articles.title: Germany Has Entered the Populist Era - Tribunemag.co.uk
articles.summary: Germany Has Entered the Populist Era  Tribunemag.co.uk
articles.full_text:
The three regional elections held in Germany last month — two in the sparsely populated, economically embattled East, and one in the booming multicultural capital, Berlin — saw Europe’s populist wave definitively hit its largest economy. That this wave was approaching, a decade after it had swelled in Southern Europe, was already clear from the 2025 federal election, in which the left-wing Die Linke as well as the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) made notable gains. But the votes in September represent a shift from quantity to quality: a sign that German populism is here to stay.
In the eastern periphery, the AfD is now far and above the strongest force in politics. In Berlin, a bellwether for the political mood in other large urban areas, Die Linke is now in the lead (even if that lead is much smaller than that of its far-right rivals). We may still be a ways off from the ‘candle burning at both ends’ metaphor used to describe the ill-fated Weimar Republic, destabilised by the Nazis on the one end and Communists on the other, but a new era of polarisation — and, as a result, institutional instability — appears to have dawned in the Federal Republic. As the middle erodes, both the right and left are putting forward contrasting ideas of what ‘democracy’ means. Which of them ultimately wins out will help to determine the country’s political future.
The AfD has led the polls across the country for some time now, a trend that shows little sign of reversing as Friedrich Merz’s government continues its political freefall. In last month’s elections the right-populist party definitely established itself as the leading force in the East, taking nearly 45 percent of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, followed by some 38 percent in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania. For the AfD’s opponents in the ‘democratic’ camp — all of whom, with the partial exception of Die Linke, have seen their support crater — it is becoming increasingly difficult to justify the party’s exclusion from power on democratic grounds.
Much has been written in both the mainstream and left-wing press about the extent to which fears of mass migration and generalised xenophobia motivate AfD voters, as opposed to the experience of economic decline and political frustration. The precise contours of that motivation certainly vary according to region and electoral demographic, but in those areas where the AfD is within striking distance of an absolute majority, its support has come to resemble what in US politics is sometimes referred to as a ‘fuck-you vote’. Similar to support for Trump or the slim majority for Brexit in 2016, rather than an expression of firm right-wing political hegemony, the AfD functions as a lightning rod for frustrations of every stripe — a gigantic middle finger aimed at all those perceived to be responsible for the country’s malaise.
Without a doubt, the success of right-populisms across the West testifies to the growing influence of right-wing ideology as it fills the vacuum left by the neoliberal centre. Nevertheless, this new right remains fragile and at times incoherent in Germany as elsewhere. Perhaps even more so than left-populism, right-populism leans heavily on charismatic leaders: a role which, in Germany, has now been filled by Ulrich Siegmund, the AfD’s poster boy in Saxony-Anhalt whose seemingly effortless charm and ability to weaponise a kind of East German identity politics has led more than one observer to sardonically refer to him as the ‘Mamdani of Magdeburg’. In Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the AfD lacks such a figure, and relied heavily on appearances by Siegmund in the final weeks of the campaign. (The Social Democrats meanwhile ran a heavily personalised campaign around Minister-President Manuela Schwesig, perhaps the party’s last genuinely popular politician in Germany, and came in close second.)
Precisely because of its ideologically fragmented character, the track record of right-wing populist governments is mixed. Although they tend to hold onto power longer than their left-wing counterparts, they ultimately suffer from the same dilemma: once they form a government, they cease to be the ‘fuck-you vote’ and begin to bleed support. The AfD leadership seems to be aware of this danger. Its figureheads in the East, like Siegmund or Tino Chrupalla, party leader in Brandenburg, avoid addressing substantive policy by redirecting focus to the so-called ‘democracy question’. ‘The AfD is a democracy project’, the refrain goes, arguing that with election results like these, keeping them out of government is untenable and indeed anti-democratic. It is an exercise in self-victimisation, rather than political agenda setting. And — one has to hand it to them — it works.
The ‘fuck-you’ strategy may soon run its course, however, after the AfD took its first step towards government by appointing a president of the state parliament with the votes of Sahra Wagenknecht’s BSW. By governing, the AfD would be forced to choose between the conflicting class interests within its own ranks. While racism and ‘remigration’ could continue to act as the ideological glue that binds the party together for a while, even the most barbaric migration policy will fail to repair a single bridge, prevent a single factory closure, or fund a single school. It’s not hard to imagine the social grievances currently driving the AfD’s rise becoming its Achilles’ heel in government. That said, they would have ample opportunity to inflict immense damage in the meantime.
Die Linke’s electoral result in Berlin, winning nearly 26 percent of the vote and taking first place in the capital for the first time, was even better than its supporters predicted, opening up new prospects for the party to play an influential role in national politics. But it forms only one part of a significantly more mixed picture. Whereas the AfD is making impressive gains virtually everywhere across Germany, Die Linke’s success is confined to Berlin — it suffered further historic defeats in its former Eastern strongholds. Last spring’s state elections in western Germany, while not ‘defeats’ in the strict sense, as the party’s overall vote total increased slightly, were hardly cause for celebration.
The party now faces a clear fork in the road. In the Eastern states, it continues to hew to moderate positions and portray itself as a competent administrator with vague slogans such as ‘A Home for Everyone’ and — incredibly — ‘Reliable Governance’. In Berlin, by contrast, although the campaign was also oriented towards governing, it tapped into a left-populist, anti-elite rhetoric and advanced clear demands on housing that successfully polarised the electorate. It came across as combative, as a force intent on driving change from within government, whereas in Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, the party essentially promised that things would stay just as they are.
The implications for the national party are obvious: the strategy pursued by the party’s new leadership over the past two years, combining a sharper rhetorical edge with a strong focus on door-to-door campaigning and grassroots organising, is bearing fruit. The success in Berlin provides its proponents with a compelling argument to push harder for shifts in campaign strategy and political direction. Complacency, particularly in the provinces, is a path to irrelevance.
For better or worse, this organisational reorientation will now have to take place alongside forming a state government. Granted, this time around, Die Linke will be the leading force in the coalition for the first time, but it will nevertheless have to contend with significant financial constraints, not to mention partners seemingly more intent on sabotaging rather than boosting that partnership. Such a task would prove challenging for the most robust socialist party, but it will be even more difficult for what remains in many ways an embryonic left-populism, as it risks forfeiting the very protest vote that brought it to power in the first place — a fate that has already befallen several of Die Linke’s sister parties across Europe.
In the best-case scenario, Die Linke — unlike the far more contradictory AfD — could leverage tangible material gains on the one hand and consolidate its extra-parliamentary influence on the other to forge its 25 percent in Berlin into a lasting coalition that serves as the basis for further growth. This requires, more than anything else, that Berlin’s left-wing government actually delivers those improvements, while the party leadership must honour its commitment to rebuilding the party into a political fighting machine.
One perhaps reassuring development is the abject fear the prospect of such a government has struck into the hearts of the powers that be. Since election night, Die Linke has been the target of a wall-to-wall smear campaign centred largely around accusations of antisemitism due to its support for Palestine, with everyone from newspaper editors to government ministers joining the fray. The objective of this frantic handwaving is clear: to keep the party out of government, lest it act on its promise to bring hundreds of thousands of housing units back into public hands — a move voters supported overwhelmingly five years ago, but has been studiously ignored by every administration since.
So far, Berliners appear unimpressed: support for Die Linke remains stable, as does support for it forming a government. Nevertheless, this window of opportunity likely won’t remain open for long. After all, a populist moment like the one Germany is currently experiencing is defined by instability and unpredictability within the electoral system. For now, however, the Left has, if not the opportunity, then at least the mandate to put its own vision of democracy into practice, at least in one city-state.

articles.full_text:
Brussels – Following the latest rise in interest rates decided at the September meeting, the European Central Bank may be considering a pause, possibly a prolonged one. This is less a matter of speculation than a necessity to safeguard the eurozone economy. The reason is that, as the ECB’s Executive Board concludes, “a further rise in long-term interest rates could adversely affect growth.“ This is probably one of the key passages in the minutes of the meeting of 10 September, when interest rates were raised.
Among the many factors and various indicators discussed at the meeting, the ECB ultimately appears to have taken into account the impact of monetary policy decisions on the overall performance of the eurozone. The stated objective of maintaining price stability and combating rising inflation now appears to clash with the need to avoid exacerbating the situation. With the ECB leaning towards a pause to avert adverse effects on businesses, households and investors, it is now up to national governments to take action.
“Structural reform remained necessary to support higher potential growth,” according to the position expressed by the members of the ECB’s Governing Council. In this regard, general concern has been expressed about “the continued weak momentum of reform efforts” and “the time lags involved,” which are seen as counterproductive factors, preventing potential reforms from being regarded as “an upside risk factor.”
On the subject of reforms, in this renewed call to speed up political action, the ECB’s Governing Council urges that public finances be kept in order. According to the minutes of the September meeting, “it was noted that the recent increase in public spending and the rise in long-term government bond yields could add to vulnerabilities over time.” Consequently, “it is important to maintain sound public finances.” This message appears to contrast with Italy’s call for greater flexibility on spending.

articles.title: ECB policymakers, accounts dampen near-term rate hike bets - The Mighty 790 KFGO
articles.summary: ECB policymakers, accounts dampen near-term rate hike bets  The Mighty 790 KFGO
articles.full_text:
By Balazs Koranyi
FRANKFURT, Oct 8 (Reuters) – Euro zone inflation could go higher than already-elevated projections, but policymakers dampened near-term rate hike bets on Thursday, arguing that underlying trends reveal a more benign picture.
The ECB raised interest rates twice this summer and markets are betting on two or three more moves as inflation is already almost twice the bank’s 2% target and could still go higher as expensive energy bites.
A long list of policymakers speaking in different corners of Europe all pointed to some comforting price trends, however, suggesting that they are not in a rush to hike again.
They argued that all of the inflation surge was due to higher energy prices, and said dangerous second-round effects that could prolong inflation have been negligible.
Longer term price expectations remain firmly anchored while higher yields on European government bonds and waning support from fiscal policy will all weigh on price growth in the months ahead, the policymakers added.
“More stable behaviour of core inflation provides some reassurance that broader inflationary pressures remain contained,” Slovenian central bank chief Primoz Dolenc told Reuters. “As regards to second-round effects from high energy inflation to wages, we haven’t seen that yet.”
Greece’s Yannis Stournaras and the Netherlands’ Olaf Sleijpen both said medium- and longer-term inflation expectations, which are most relevant for the ECB, remain well anchored around the target.
“This is good. So we should take this into account and be moderate in our monetary policy,” Stournaras told a financial conference in Istanbul.
ECB chief economist Philip Lane, speaking in London, argued that support from fiscal policy, a key factor in relatively robust economic growth this year, is likely to wane in 2027, dampening both expansion and inflationary pressures.
Accounts released on Thursday of the ECB’s September 9-10 policy meeting nevertheless showed all policymakers agreed that inflation risks are skewed towards even higher readings given exceptional volatility in energy and pervasive uncertainty.
The comments appear consistent with the finding of a Reuters poll, which showed that nearly all of the 73 economists surveyed see the ECB on hold this month, with the vast majority anticipating a move only in December.
“Persistently elevated inflation that we see in our September projection and the lack of resolution of conflicts in the Middle East, Ukraine and elsewhere, supports the case for moving policy rates towards a more restrictive territory,” Dolenc said.
“But when and by how much we will determine on a meeting-by-meeting basis, based on the incoming data.”

The European Central Bank (ECB) is expected to leave interest rates unchanged in October before delivering another increase in December, according to a Reuters poll conducted October 5-8.
The survey shows that 70 of 73 economists expect the ECB to hold its deposit rate at 2.50% on October 29, while 64 of 73 anticipate a 25-basis-point (bps) hike in December. A 58% majority expect the deposit rate to peak at 2.75%. However, 24 economists see rates reaching 3.00%, up from just two last month.
The ECB has raised rates twice this year as higher Oil prices stemming from the war in the Middle East have pushed inflation above its 2% target.
Economists now expect inflation to average 3.7% in the fourth quarter, up from 3.3% in the third quarter and above the 3.3% forecast in last month’s survey. Annual inflation forecasts have also been revised higher, to 3.0% in 2026 and 2.6% in 2027, compared with previous estimates of 2.9% and 2.3%, respectively.
The Eurozone economy is expected to grow by 1.0% this year, up from 0.8% in the previous survey. Growth is forecast at 1.2% in 2027 and 1.3% in 2028.
ECB FAQs
The European Central Bank (ECB) in Frankfurt, Germany, is the reserve bank for the Eurozone. The ECB sets interest rates and manages monetary policy for the region. The ECB primary mandate is to maintain price stability, which means keeping inflation at around 2%. Its primary tool for achieving this is by raising or lowering interest rates. Relatively high interest rates will usually result in a stronger Euro and vice versa. The ECB Governing Council makes monetary policy decisions at meetings held eight times a year. Decisions are made by heads of the Eurozone national banks and six permanent members, including the President of the ECB, Christine Lagarde.
In extreme situations, the European Central Bank can enact a policy tool called Quantitative Easing. QE is the process by which the ECB prints Euros and uses them to buy assets – usually government or corporate bonds – from banks and other financial institutions. QE usually results in a weaker Euro. QE is a last resort when simply lowering interest rates is unlikely to achieve the objective of price stability. The ECB used it during the Great Financial Crisis in 2009-11, in 2015 when inflation remained stubbornly low, as well as during the covid pandemic.
Quantitative tightening (QT) is the reverse of QE. It is undertaken after QE when an economic recovery is underway and inflation starts rising. Whilst in QE the European Central Bank (ECB) purchases government and corporate bonds from financial institutions to provide them with liquidity, in QT the ECB stops buying more bonds, and stops reinvesting the principal maturing on the bonds it already holds. It is usually positive (or bullish) for the Euro.

articles.title: Far-right rise threatens Europe’s rearmament efforts and support for Ukraine - وكالة الأنباء السورية – سانا
articles.summary: Far-right rise threatens Europe’s rearmament efforts and support for Ukraine  وكالة الأنباء السورية – سانا
articles.full_text:
Capitals, Oct. 8 (SANA) European efforts to strengthen defense capabilities and rearm are facing growing political challenges as far-right parties gain popularity by capitalizing on concerns over rising living costs to oppose increased military spending and aid to Ukraine, according to a report by U.S. magazine Politico.
Far-right parties in France, Italy, Germany, Poland, Romania and Belgium are seeking to turn public discontent over economic pressures into opposition to aid to Kyiv, increases in defense budgets or an expanded European Union role in defense, despite differences in their positions on these issues.
Livelihoods vs. Defense Spending
Last month, Marine Le Pen, leader of France’s National Rally, called for limiting aid to Ukraine, saying France could no longer afford to continue providing such support.
In Italy, Roberto Vannacci, a former general and leader of the far-right National Future party, called for a rethink of defense spending, arguing that increased military spending was unjustified at a time when prices of basic goods are rising.
The positions put European governments and mainstream political parties in a difficult position as they seek to maintain public support for higher defense spending while military budgets compete with social welfare and public services.
Janne Kuusela, permanent secretary at Finland’s Ministry of Defence, said rising living costs are creating room for “populist rhetoric” over the scale of financial support that should be provided to Ukraine and the investments required for defense.
The positions of European far-right parties on defense generally fall into three categories: opposition to military aid to Ukraine, rejection of joint defense projects at the EU level, and criticism of increased defense spending.
France’s National Rally and Romania’s Alliance for the Union of Romanians, or AUR, oppose aid to Kyiv. Poland’s Law and Justice party, or PiS, and the Netherlands’ Party for Freedom, or PVV, oppose EU-level defense projects, while Germany’s Alternative for Germany, or AfD, and Italy’s National Future criticize increased defense spending more broadly.
Critics of these parties argue that their positions could serve Moscow’s interests. German Defense Minister Boris Pistorius said the pressure exerted by the right “does not actually come from the right itself, but mostly from Moscow.”
Pressure and Implications for European Security
The gains made by far-right parties are placing centrist parties under growing pressure to defend plans to increase military spending or seek cuts to maintain public support.
The challenge is becoming more significant as elections approach in 2027 in several major NATO member states, including France, Italy and Poland, while governments prepare next year’s budgets.
Slower defense spending could threaten NATO efforts to meet its target of allocating 5 percent of gross domestic product to defense and security by 2035.
A NATO military official said the alliance “is in a position where it needs to catch up with Russia,” warning that a halt in support could result in the loss of some capabilities.
European countries and Canada are expected to spend about $634 billion on core defense needs this year, an 11 percent increase from 2025, according to the report. However, an August poll by the European Council on Foreign Relations found that 46.2 percent of respondents in eight European countries opposed increasing defense spending if it required higher taxes, compared with 35.5 percent who supported such an increase. Opposition was higher in Germany, France, Italy, Spain and Poland.
An internal NATO poll also showed public support for backing Ukraine declining from 59 percent in 2025 to 55 percent this year, with direct military assistance the least popular form of support.
The political pressure is already affecting defense policy in some countries. In Italy, Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni proposed last week cutting defense spending by about €8 billion from the government’s initial proposal under pressure from the League, her coalition partner.
In Poland, President Karol Nawrocki, backed by the Law and Justice party, sought to prevent his country from accessing nearly €44 billion in EU defense loans, warning that the scheme could increase Poland’s dependence on Brussels and burden future generations with debt.
NATO officials and diplomats fear that slower spending by major countries could weaken funding for the military capabilities needed to deter Russia, particularly as France and Italy account for a significant share of defense investment and assistance to Ukraine.
A NATO diplomat said that if major countries stopped making progress, this would affect the alliance’s and Europe’s ability to defend themselves and leave Ukraine more vulnerable.
Guntram Wolff, a senior fellow and defense economics analyst at the Brussels-based Bruegel think tank, said pressure to rethink defense spending could also affect the amount earmarked for defense in the EU’s next long-term budget if negotiations continue into next year.
Europe’s battle over rearmament, therefore, appears linked not only to securing military resources and capabilities but also to governments’ ability to maintain public support for increased defense spending amid economic pressures and the rise of political movements that place national and social priorities against collective security commitments and support for Ukraine, according to Politico.

articles.title: ‘This is a crisis of hope’: Echoes of 1968 as France’s students rise up - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: ‘This is a crisis of hope’: Echoes of 1968 as France’s students rise up  Al JazeeraFrench ministers scramble to appease students after 10 days of protests  The GuardianFrance's school protests: What lies behind the anger  BBCFrench students keep up protest pressure with some demonstrations hit by violence  ReutersPolitics  The Economist
articles.full_text:
The scale of protests raging across France over the education system, attracting hundreds of thousands of pupils, teachers and parents, has been described as exceptional by unions and student movement organisers.
“I think this is very historic and unprecedented by how big it is,” Alice Cohen-Morzadec, international spokesperson for France’s Student Union, said on Tuesday, when government sources put the number of protesters at 266,000.
“Some are saying this is the biggest movement since May 1968,” she added.
The student protests at Paris universities nearly five decades ago were initially driven by opposition to an outdated and overcrowded system, limited opportunities and broader political concerns.
The unrest soon spread beyond campuses, expanding into nationwide strikes involving millions of workers that virtually paralysed the country.
Back then, President Charles de Gaulle was in power. Today’s protests come as France heads into next year’s presidential elections, which are being eyed by the far right.
As in 1968, the protests that started on September 21 at an underdeveloped Paris suburban high school are about funding for education, teacher shortages, overcrowded classes, and school facilities.
But those are triggers and not the deeper causes, according to historians and student movement organisers.
“For the young people, this is a crisis of hope. You can see they are bombarded daily with economic problems, political extremes, dangers of warfare in Europe, the threat to their careers from AI, high youth unemployment rates, the climate crisis,” Andrew Smith, historian of modern France and lecturer in Liberal Arts at Queen Mary University of London, told Al Jazeera.
He said students are dissatisfied because of a lack of substantive interaction between the government and student representatives and unions in recent years.
“It has been difficult for the government to meet with interlocutors and try to have dialogue with social partners,” he said.
Robi Morder, a researcher on social movements in France, said the lack of communication reflects the current government’s approach.
“In 1990 and 1998, governments were led by socialists and leftists. Some of the ministers had been in the youth movement. So when there was an issue, the government knew how to negotiate. In 1990, the president himself received a delegation of students,” said Morder.
“We are not in the same situation because the government is not only from the other side politically, but they also don’t have the experience of the old political class,” he added. “They don’t know how to negotiate a social conflict. The government’s first answer is, ‘It is nothing; we will call the police, and everything will be OK.’”
Student organisers say they are frustrated because they feel the government is not taking them seriously.
“This is too much. Enough is enough. We have been making these demands for years. We need more money for education, we need more teachers, we need better facilities,” said Chloe Grunenwald, vice president of the Federation of the General Association of Students (FAGE), the largest organisation of its kind in France, representing some 300,000 students.
When interviewed by Al Jazeera, several students said they had joined recent protests in solidarity with those who first took to the streets. The broadening of the coalition is illustrated by the fact that both Grunenwald and Cohen-Morzadec represent university unions rallying in support of high school pupils.
Smith and Morder spoke of the differences between now and 1968.
“This school year started very differently. The never-ending heatwaves is one thing that really provoked it and made it catch fire. We had classrooms with over 40 people in temperatures exceeding 40 degrees [Celsius;104 Fahrenheit]. That is untenable,” Smith said.
Alleged police brutality
Protest organisers and unions have also complained about what they see as police brutality.
“Unfortunately, the media are talking about how bins are being burnt, schools are being blocked, and how it is a form of violence. The real violence is actually coming from the government side,” said Cohen-Morzadec.
In a sign of conciliation, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu on Wednesday said, “Students must be heard,” while Interior Minister Laurent Nunez ordered police to suspend the use of stun grenades against protesting high school pupils.
But those moves might not be enough to calm the anger.
“We are going to mobilise until we get our demands, especially because we have October 17 and November 20 – as an international date for the youth in all Europe to mobilise for our future, so we want to continue at least until those dates, if not further,” said Cohen-Morzadec.
Nationwide strikes and antigovernment demonstrations are scheduled for October 17, expected to bring together a large number of unions to air their grievances against soaring energy and food prices, proposed budget cuts, and freezes on public sector salaries.
The strikes are backed by the left-wing France Unbowed (LFI) party, led by Jean-Luc Melenchon, and the country’s main labour union, known by its French acronym, CGT.
Critics have accused the LFI and Melenchon of inciting violence to score points against the government, an accusation they and protest organisers deny.
“Our message has been the same. We are fighting for our rights and our demonstrations are passive. We are not working on behalf of anyone else,” said Grunenwald.
Student unions have published a list of 10 demands they say will cost the government 1 billion euros ($1.1bn), and have promised to keep up the pressure until all those requirements are met.
Among the demands are calls for greater investment in schools and universities and more staff and space in higher education. Students are calling for stronger financial and housing support, affordable university meals, and an end to higher fees for international students. They also want an end to what they call “all forms of repression linked to the high school and student movement”.

A Russian glide bomb killed dozens of Ukrainians at a bus stop in the eastern city of Kramatorsk on Thursday, in one of the deadliest attacks on civilians in recent months.
Two buses were hit by the bomb during rush hour, killing at least 30 people and injuring 18, according to Ukraine’s state emergency service. A separate attack nearby killed another three people, authorities said.
“Some of those killed have still not been identified because of the severity of their injuries,” President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said. Many of those injured in the attack were fighting for their lives, he said, warning that the death toll may rise.
The strike came after Zelenskyy told the FT last week that Vladimir Putin had instructed his generals to abandon all rules of war in Ukraine. Deliberately targeting civilians is considered a war crime under international law.
Russia has used aerial bombs since its full-scale invasion in 2022, launching them from behind the front line to destroy entire buildings.
“Russia is systematically destroying Kramatorsk and terrorising civilians,” Dmytro Lubinets, the Ukrainian parliament’s commissioner for human rights, wrote on X.
Regional governor Vadym Filashkin said in a post on Telegram that the victims “are not ‘the consequences of war’, nor dry statistics. These are people killed by the Russian army.”
He said that public transport in Kramatorsk and the neighbouring city of Slovyansk had been suspended because of the threat of Russian attacks.
The bus stop bombing came a day after a wave of Russian missiles and drones killed at least 28 people across Ukraine, including 22 in an attack on an apartment building in Pryluky, about 150km east of Kyiv.
The building suffered a direct hit from a Russian missile, burying residents beneath debris. Dozens of injured people were pulled out by rescuers — as were the lifeless bodies of four children. In Kyiv, three people were killed in Wednesday’s strikes, the capital’s mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
The combined death toll from Russian strikes over the past day and a half has risen to at least 64 people.
On Thursday, sirens howled throughout Kyiv as explosions from Russian drone strikes and Ukrainian air defence interceptions shook the city’s buildings. A blanket of dense black smoke was visible over the capital around midday.
DTEK, Ukraine’s largest energy operator, said that it had imposed power cuts in Kyiv and the surrounding region after Russian strikes hit its energy facilities for a second straight day.
Zelenskyy told the FT Putin was also increasing his attacks on civilians because the Russian army had failed to achieve its military goals on the battlefield.
Ukrainian forces have made gains along the eastern frontline in the Donbas in recent weeks, thwarting Russian efforts to encircle Kramatorsk and nearby cities that make up Ukraine’s “fortress belt”, according to military analysts who track the war.
“Over the month of September, the Russian net gains were negative 190km²,” the Finland-based Black Bird Group, which tracks the war, reported last week. “This marks the greatest monthly net territorial loss for Russia in our dataset since the June of 2023.”
Zelenskyy said last week the counteroffensive, dubbed Operation Vivaldi, had liberated some 125-140 sq km of territory.
Putin has demanded that Ukraine give up the remaining 25 per cent of the Donbas region still under its control to even begin peace talks. US President Donald Trump and his special envoy Steve Witkoff have also pushed Kyiv to hand over the land in order to bring Putin back to the negotiating table.
But Zelenskyy has insisted that territorial concessions are a red line for Kyiv and said that giving the Donbas to Russia would only aid Putin’s army in its broader goal of launching attacks deeper inside Ukraine to bring it to heel. Ukrainian polling throughout the war has supported his stance.
On Thursday, while visiting Pryluky with UK foreign secretary Ed Miliband, Zelenskyy said his negotiating team would travel this week to the US to meet Trump’s team to discuss strategy around peace negotiations. The Ukrainian leader also called on the US to increase pressure on Putin to end his war.

VIENNA — German lawmakers on Thursday approved the acquisition of four additional MEKO A-200 DEU frigates from shipbuilder TKMS, bringing Berlin’s planned fleet to eight ships after the government abandoned its troubled F126 program.
The Bundestag budget committee had approved the first four vessels July 8, alongside an option for four more. The Defense Ministry said the decision to exercise that option will give the German Navy a single, eight-ship class intended chiefly for anti-submarine warfare.
Delivery of the first vessel is set for 2029, the agency said in a statement. The ships will support NATO missions in the Baltic and North seas, the Atlantic and the High North, according to the announcement.
Berlin selected the MEKO design after withdrawing from its contract with Damen Naval for six F126 frigates, which had initially been intended to supply the Navy’s future anti-submarine warfare capability. The ministry attributed its withdrawal to “considerable performance problems” by Damen, saying it had completed a broader assessment before terminating the arrangement.
The program change has already triggered a costly dispute. Damen is seeking €4.7 billion ($5.3 billion) in damages from the German government, arguing that Berlin’s termination was politically motivated and legally unfounded, Der Spiegel reported last week. The F126 effort had already cost Germany more than €2 billion without delivering a ship, according to public broadcaster ARD.
The initial four-ship MEKO purchase carried a reported €6.3 billion price tag, while the four-ship option was valued at €5.3 billion. Reuters reported that the second tranche, including project support and reserves, would cost roughly €5.6 billion; the projected operating costs for those four vessels through 2045 amount to another €1.55 billion.
The Defense Ministry argued that selecting one ship type should simplify training, maintenance and logistics. It also said variants of the MEKO A-200 are already in service with allied navies.
TKMS described the envisioned eight-ship production run as the company’s largest-ever surface vessel contract.
“With the four frigates already on order, the program has entered the implementation phase,” the shipbuilder said in a statement.
As part of its post-2022 buildup, the German military has put a heavy emphasis on anti-submarine warfare abilities in the Baltic, North Sea and, especially since the crisis over Greenland, in the Arctic. The F-126 was meant to be an integral part of this strategy. Other, more successful, procurements aimed at combating submarines include the Boeing P-8A Poseidon maritime-surveillance aircraft, the first of which landed in Germany almost exactly a year ago.
Linus Höller is Defense News' Europe correspondent and OSINT investigator. He reports on the arms deals, sanctions, and geopolitics shaping Europe and the world. He holds master’s degrees in WMD nonproliferation, terrorism studies, and international relations, and works in four languages: English, German, Russian, and Spanish.

articles.title: ECB May Hike Further as Inflation Risks Persist, Dolenc Says - Global Banking & Finance Review

ECB May Need Further Rate Hikes Amid Persistent Inflation Risks
ECB Policymaker Discusses Interest Rate Outlook and Inflation Concerns
By Balazs Koranyi
LJUBLJANA, Oct 8 (Reuters) - The European Central Bank may have to keep raising interest rates given an abundance of upside inflation risks but the timing and size of any move remain far too uncertain to predict, ECB policymaker Primoz Dolenc said.
The ECB can also take some comfort in the composition of inflation data, which shows only a limited pass-through of high energy costs to other goods and services, and suggests no second-round effect on wages, Dolenc, Slovenia's central bank chief, said in an interview.
Recent ECB Rate Hikes and Inflation Data
The ECB has raised its deposit rate twice this year to 2.5% as inflation jumped to nearly twice its 2% target last month and policymakers are now scrutinising the data to determine just how much more tightening is needed to prevent an Iran-war induced energy cost surge from getting embedded.
"Persistently elevated inflation that we see in our September projection and the lack of resolution of conflicts in the Middle East, Ukraine and elsewhere, supports the case for moving policy rates towards a more restrictive territory," Dolenc said. "But when and by how much we will determine on a meeting-by-meeting basis, based on the incoming data."
Core Inflation Trends
While last month's 3.8% inflation reading was above expectations, it was largely driven by energy, a volatile indicator, and underlying figures pointed to a more comforting trend.
"Core inflation has remained relatively stable, suggesting limited pass-through to underlying inflation components, particularly services," Dolenc said. "A more stable behaviour of core inflation provides some reassurance that broader inflationary pressures remain contained."
Risks Skewed Towards Higher Inflation
Energy and Food Price Concerns
Still, risks are skewed towards higher price readings, he argued.
Energy prices could still go higher while low natural gas storage levels in the run-up to the winter are a worry, since any jump in wholesale gas prices gets transmitted to retail prices more quickly, Dolenc said.
Food prices could also rise on the combination of high input costs, droughts and El Niño, and even the euro zone's unexpectedly strong economic performance is a potential inflationary risk.
Economic Performance and Growth Risks
The energy price surge was expected to wipe out most of the bloc's growth this year but the economy is showing the sort of resilience seen in previous crises and it grew at its quickest rate in four years in the second quarter, well above its potential.
Since much of this was driven by personal consumption and services spending, the solid performance is likely to persist, as suggested by survey indicators, Dolenc said.
Impact of Borrowing Costs and Market Reactions
A key growth risk may be the recent rise in longer-term borrowing costs and ECB board members Philip Lane and Isabel Schnabel have both warned that the jump in yields could hold back the economy more than predicted.
Financial analysts are especially worried about the rising premium investors demand to hold French debt and some are discussing whether the ECB would intervene in markets.
Monetary Policy Transmission
Dampening those expectations, Dolenc said monetary policy continues to be transmitted to the economy efficiently.
"Monetary policy is transmitted more or less homogeneously into broader financial conditions all over the euro area," he said. "We haven't seen any destructive effect of rising yields on other parts of the economy."

articles.title: 'The Orange Plague': Naked Trump statue on display at European Parliament in Strasbourg - Euronews.com
articles.summary: 'The Orange Plague': Naked Trump statue on display at European Parliament in Strasbourg  Euronews.com‘King of Injustice’: Golden naked Trump statue installed at European Parliament  CNNArtist unveils golden statue of a nude Donald Trump at European parliament building  The Art NewspaperNaked Trump statue goes on display in Strasbourg  DW.comWhat the grotesque ‘naked Trump’ statue tells us about the UK’s future back in Europe  The Independent
articles.full_text:
A gold statue depicting Donald Trump fully naked and crushing a smaller man’s shoulders has been unveiled in the European Parliament building in Strasbourg, France.
A new statue has been introduced to the European Parliament building in Strasbourg, and it’s all kinds of satirical and naked.
Titled "The Orange Plague," the 2.6-meter statue by Danish artist Jens Galschiøt, is a depiction of a nude Donald Trump holding a comically sized golf club in one hand, a set of scales in the other, all while sitting on the back of a smaller, frailer man.
The artist said it is coated with 23-karat gold and that his work is also known by the name "King of Injustice."
Beneath the statue is a plaque which reads:
"I am sitting on the back of a man.
He is sinking under my burden
I will do anything to help him.
Except stepping down from his back.
- The King of Injustice."
According to Galschiøt, the work was inspired by Hans Christian Andersen’s The Emperor’s New Clothes, and is a “satirical outcry” against Trump’s volatile climate and foreign policies.
“Nations as well as NGOs are afraid to openly raise the subject [of] how to deal with Trump and his policies, fearing tariffs, fund-cuts, deportations or the like,” Galschiøt wrote on his website. “As an independent art workshop we are not restricted by such bonds. This sculpture has been made to address ‘the elephant in the room’ and start a necessary debate [about] how the US is destroying the world’s only chance to counter the climate catastrophe.”
All visitors receive a 3D-printed miniature of the sculpture to take home.
Galschiøt has said he printed around 20,000 sculptures that he distributed not only to visitors but also to staff throughout the European Parliament.
Left-wing Danish European Parliament member Per Clausen, who invited the artist, said he is not worried about a potential reaction by Trump.
"If someone is so thin-skinned that they cannot tolerate this sculpture being exhibited in the European Parliament, then they have no place on the world stage," Clausen said.
As of yet, no reaction from the subject of “The Orange Plague", who is usually reactive online and not known for his thick skin in these matters.
The statue was previously displayed at the “hands off Greenland” demonstrations in Copenhagen earlier this year and the COP30 UN Climate Summit in Belém, Brazil last year.
After the present installation in Strasbourg, Galschiøt plans to exhibit "The Orange Plague" again at the COP31 UN Climate Conference next month Antalya, Türkiye.

articles.summary: Deutsche Bank’s most legendary trader has a big day coming  eFinancialCareersBarclays traders’ convictions quashed after Supreme Court ruling  The TimesEx-bankers jailed for rigging rates have convictions quashed  BBCEx-trader to sue Barclays over Libor rigging case  The TelegraphFormer City traders’ fraud convictions overturned  City AM
articles.full_text:
Morning Coffee: Deutsche Bank’s most legendary trader has a big day coming. Hedge fund manager loses billions but gets another $1.5bn back
“Having this conviction quashed is not simply about correcting the record, it’s about finally having validation that this is an injustice that never should have happened”. Jonathan Mathew spoke eloquently for his fellow former Barclays rates traders yesterday, as their criminal convictions for fixing the LIBOR market ten years ago were quashed.
It is maybe not quite as complete a vindication as he might have implied while hugging his lawyer – the Serious Fraud Office was keen to remind everyone that the reason for quashing the convictions was that there had been errors in the judge’s guidance ten years ago and that it’s not clear that they might not have been convicted anyway if that mistake had not been made. But be that as it may, the SFO seems to be of the view that it’s water under the bridge, the LIBOR market itself no longer exists and that consequently there’s no point in spending anyone’s time and money relitigating the 2010s. Barclays also decided not to make any comment.
All of which means that – since his case turns on exactly the same point of law – former Deutsche trader Christian Bittar will also soon be celebrating on the courtroom steps this Friday. Bittar was only second to Tom Hayes himself in terms of his prominence in the LIBOR scandal – he famously made nearly EUR2bn in revenue for Deutsche Bank over a five year period, and received a $140m bonus in 2008. Bittar was sentenced to five years after pleading guilty in 2018, and has been appealing his conviction ever since the Supreme Court found that Hayes had been subject to a miscarriage of justice.
The question is, what next? Tom Hayes is currently suing his former employer, UBS, in the Connecticut courts, and the sums of money ($400m) involved are large even for someone like Bittar. The most recent filing in Hayes' case is a long memo from UBS setting out the case that co-operating with law enforcement is protected free speech, but if he’s in the mood for revenge, Bittar might do something similar.
Or he could get back into the market. With a quashed conviction, there’s nothing to stop Christian Bittar from returning to the financial services industry, and not so long ago there were hedge funds competing for his services. Bittar has a slight problem in that his experience as a short term interest futures trader might not be considered relevant given the substantial changes in market structure as a result of the LIBOR debacle. But he was genuinely regarded as a legend on the Deutsche trading desk, and there are plenty of his former colleagues who are still in the market and possibly able to vouch for him.
Alternatively, Bittar might choose to accept the clearing of his name, to be philosophical about the 23 months’ incarceration that he can’t get back, and get on with the rest of his life. After (presumably) opening a bottle of champagne and giving a short statement to the media, Christian Bittar will have a lot to think about this weekend.
Elsewhere, it’s not exactly “easy come, easy go”, but in the world of hedge funds it has to be some consolation while going through a period of bad returns to know that they are not (or at least, not yet) impairing your ability to raise funds. Hamza Lessougeur’s Arini Capital has had a tough time of it this year, with the flagship fund down 16%. But nonetheless, it’s raised $1.5bn in another fund.
This is partly because the fund that’s got the new money is Arini’s credit strategy, a highly concentrated fund which has been closed for years. Although 2026 has been a lousy environment for general credit investment, with situations like Altice and Aston Martin weighing on the market, it seems that investors still have confidence in Lessougeur.
It just goes to underline the wisdom of not always trying to maximise fee income. As well as keeping its size manageable so as not to drag on performance, closing the credit fund creates pent-up demand, and an investor base that will be prepared to subscribe even when others might be looking at the performance numbers and asking questions. Just like in show business, it’s best to leave them wanting more.
Meanwhile …
“I’m hopeful that it slows down and gets delayed … I’m not sure we’ve seen that much of it”. According to David Friedland of Citi, last year’s interruption in the poaching of junior staff by private equity has not continued into a trend. He also admitted that his 23 year-old son’s group chats had lit up this week with the big news about Citi’s graduate program. (Bloomberg)
Jane Dunlevie has been promoted from Chief Operating Officer of the TMT investment banking group at Goldman Sachs to be one of three co-heads with Jung Min and Barry O’Brien. (Finextra)
Stories of big team moves are always fascinating, and Gabriel Boghossian has been unusually open about how he organised his private equity secondaries legal team to go from Stephenson Harwood to A&O Sherman. Among the nuggets of information – they called it “Project Gunner” after their favourite football team, and they didn’t involve any headhunters because they were worried about conflicts of interest. (Financial News)
OpenAI have dropped the solutions to hundreds of previously unsolved mathematics problems on the internet. Mathematicians are worried about what this means for the future of the subject, and whether it will continue to be a good way to demonstrate one’s potential for making loads of money at a quant fund. (WSJ)
Apparently people told Penny Pennington, the CEO of Edward Jones, that leaving a banking career to go into wealth management was “like jumping off a cliff”. (Business Insider)
It’s not really a viable status symbol for a banker (unless they have a very large country house as well), but people are now prepared to pay up to $30,000 for an elite quality sheepdog. (Bloomberg)

articles.title: El Nino set to intensify before peaking in December, UN warns - France 24
articles.summary: El Nino set to intensify before peaking in December, UN warns  France 24UN weather body says El Niño set to intensify and last until February 2027  ReutersSea-surface temperatures reflect strengthening El Niño  World Meteorological Organization WMOEl Niño to intensify before December peak - UN's World Meteorological Organization  RTE.ieThe world may never go back to how it was after this monster El Niño  New Scientist
articles.full_text:
The United Nations warned on Thursday that El Nino will intensify before peaking in December, bringing higher temperatures to much of the planet and compounding the effects of man-made climate change. The World Meteorological Organization added that this naturally occurring weather phenomenon could be the strongest since at least 1950.
El Nino will intensify even more before peaking in December, the United Nations said Thursday, warning it could be among the strongest witnessed since at least 1950.
The naturally occurring weather phenomenon is set to bring higher temperatures to much of the planet, the UN's weather and climate agency said, with its impact compounding the effects of man-made climate change.
Read moreRare train of cyclones fuelled by historic El Nino make their way across Pacific
"El Nino will continue to intensify ahead of its forecast peak in December," the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) said in its monthly Global Seasonal Climate Update.
"It is likely to bring above-average temperatures to much of the globe and shift rainfall patterns, increasing the risk of drought and floods in different regions."
El Nino warms surface temperatures in the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, bringing worldwide changes in winds, pressure and rainfall patterns.
It typically takes place every two to seven years and lasts around nine to 12 months.
Conditions oscillate between El Nino and its opposite La Nina, with neutral conditions in between.
El Nino 'strengthening rapidly'
"Sea-surface temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific are forecast to increase to record levels during October-November-December 2026, reflecting the strengthening of the El Nino event which will drive weather patterns and impact economies, ecosystems and communities across the globe," the WMO said.
The forecast is based on consensus across 13 leading national and international meteorological centres.
"El Nino is firmly established and strengthening rapidly," said WMO chief Celeste Saulo.
"WMO forecasts indicate a near-100 percent likelihood that it will persist through February 2027, potentially being one of the strongest since at least 1950."
Saulo explained that El Nino does not add new heat to the planet, but releases heat being stored in the ocean.
"The ocean it's drawing from is the warmest we've ever measured it. There is simply more heat available to release," she said.

Sea temperatures record
The index which measures sea surface temperature anomalies across the central-eastern equatorial Pacific – the region at the heart of El Nino – increased from 1.6C above normal in June to 2.5C above normal in August.
For October-November-December, the anomaly is forecast to reach approximately 3.7C above normal.
This would be the highest since observations began, eclipsing the previous record of 2.6C set in 2015-2016.
The last El Nino contributed to making 2023 the second-hottest year on record and 2024 the all-time high at around 1.55C above the 1850-1900 pre-industrial average.
While El Nino usually peaks between November and February, the resulting spike in temperatures typically comes later.
This El Nino is already hitting some regions hard, including in Central America, where animals and crops are dying from drought.

articles.summary: Tesco predicts a low-alcohol ‘healthier’ Christmas  The GuardianInterim Results 2026/27  Tesco PLCTesco predicts less boozy Christmas for UK shoppers  Financial TimesTesco expects moderation trend to curb festive alcohol sales  ReutersWeight-loss drugs lead Tesco to prepare for less boozy Christmas  The Times

Tesco has raised its profit outlook as it expects households to splash out this Christmas – despite buying less alcohol – as they shrug off “uncertainty” over the Iran war.
The UK’s biggest grocer said sales rose just 2% to £33.8bn in the 26 weeks to 29 August, but underlying profit was up 6.5% to £1.8bn.
Ken Murphy, the chief executive of Tesco, said growth had been helped by strong online sales, which were up 8%, and a 9% jump in revenue from its premium own-label Finest range.
He said: “Consumers in the UK have been pretty resilient in an uncertain environment and there is a sense that customers want to enjoy Christmas, given everything that is going on in the world.”
The retailer had bought more stock of “key Christmas lines”, understood to be foods such as turkey and mince pies, and added 10% more delivery slots for its online grocery business. It is also ramping up its in-house rapid delivery service, Whoosh, and has signed new partnerships, including with Deliveroo.
Murphy said he expected Britons to seek out a “marginally healthier Christmas” with higher sales of low-alcohol and no-alcohol drinks, including ready-mixed mocktails, but that families would still treat themselves as “customers do love to indulge”.
He said he was not expecting food supplies to be hit by this summer’s drought. Tesco had also hedged its energy costs into next year and was making savings across the business to help keep prices down for shoppers.
He said the business still had room for growth despite being almost twice the size of its nearest rival, Sainsbury’s, with a 28% market share, and that he did not “dwell too much” on the possibility of its closest rival acquiring another leading supermarket.
Sainsbury’s is understood to have walked away from merger talks in January with the UK’s sixth-biggest supermarket, Morrisons, prompting consolidation chatter across the industry.
“Whatever happens in the market we will respond to it,” Murphy said. While Tesco is expanding its reach with financial services and more fashion, he said its strategy “begins and ends in winning in food”.
The company added: “While consumer confidence has remained relatively resilient in the first half of the year, ongoing geopolitical tensions continue to create uncertainty and we remain focused on helping customers get the best possible value.”
Earlier this year, Tesco warned that profits could fall in the year ahead, citing increased uncertainty caused by the conflict in Iran, which began in late February. However, some economic indicators have suggested that the war has not yet had a significant impact. Last week, official estimates for UK growth in the second quarter were upgraded.
The company said it now expected to make underlying annual profits of between £3.15bn and £3.3bn. That represents an upgrade from its previous expectation of at least £3bn in profits but the bottom end of the range would still mark a fall from a year earlier.
Sales at established UK Tesco stores were up 1.5% as food sales motored, but the group’s Booker wholesale arm continued to struggle, with sales falling 2.6%.
The supermarket said it was increasingly using artificial intelligence across the business, including in a meal-planning assistant that was tested from April with 280,000 staff before being launched for customers in September.
It said AI was also helping to cut costs by making in-store stock replenishment more efficient and improving energy efficiency in its supermarkets.
Tesco shares rose 4% on Thursday morning.

articles.title: Protesters blame 'vulture funds' for Spain's housing crisis - BBC
articles.summary: Protesters blame 'vulture funds' for Spain's housing crisis  BBCCan Sánchez convince Spanish voters he is their best hope for fairer housing?  The GuardianSpain's rent protests could serve as warning for UK  LandlordZONEPedro Sánchez gambles on a snap election—and populist policies  The EconomistSpain approves housing decrees that triggered snap election  Reuters
articles.full_text:
- Published
Pierina Nicuray, a 21-year-old university graduate, has spent a week camped out in Madrid's Puerta del Sol square.
Like many of the hundreds of others who have pitched their tents here to protest at Spain's housing crisis, she has no doubts when it comes to diagnosing the cause.
"It's the same problem as always," she says. "A lack of homes."
She adds: "Landlords are taking advantage of the situation to raise rentals, and then there's also Airbnb."
Jorge Moreno, a 19-year-old film-dubbing student who has also been living in a tent here in central Madrid for the last few days, agrees.
"There are so many homes standing empty because they have been bought by vulture funds and investment funds which hike up the rent of people living in properties until they get rid of them," says Jorge, who lives with his mother and fears it will be a long time before he can afford a home of his own.
"They've been making a business of housing for a long time," he adds. "But it's an abusive business which stops Spaniards from being able to live in a decent home."
His and Pierina's diagnoses are frequently voiced by fellow protesters, ordinary Spaniards and even the Spanish government.
On presenting a recent package of emergency measures to tackle the housing problem, Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he was legislating "against those who consider housing just another object on the market with which to speculate".
Those reforms were rejected by Congress, prompting Sánchez to call a snap election next month.
Nicuray and Moreno can point to the single case that sparked the current Spanish housing protest movement as proof that profit-driven practices are at the heart of the crisis: the 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted from her home after the investment firm that had bought it tried to persuade her to leave, then sharply increased her rent, which she was unable to pay.
Although the social backlash that followed caused the company to invite Abascal to return to her old home, she never did, dying in hospital on Wednesday.
Many others have their own stories of struggling with a soaring rental market.
Carmen Pérez is a retired widow, originally from Ecuador, who has been living in Spain for 17 years.
When she arrived, housing was relatively cheap and accessible, but - as costs have risen - she has been forced to move in with her daughter and son-in-law as she looks for somewhere affordable to rent.
"When a property is listed to rent, there's always a long waiting list," she says. "And the rent is always too high for me. All of this has affected my health - I've got depression, I don't have any stability or security."
Spain has seen an average rise in rental costs of 84% over the last 10 years, according to property outlet Idealista.
In the centre of the southern city of Málaga, the increase has been 113 %, and, in Marbella - just under 150%.
Such numbers have made housing Spaniards' biggest concern.
A recent study by the Centre for Sociological Research (CIS) showed how the broader Spanish population, like the protesters, want to see action taken against those perceived to be powerful movers in the housing market.
Some 72% wanted higher taxes introduced for those with 10 or more properties; 76% wanted limits on short-term tourist accommodation; and 40% supported the expropriation of empty homes.
However, Jorge Galindo, director at the Esade centre for economic policy, says that available data makes it difficult to know exactly how many Spanish properties are owned by so-called "vulture funds" and being used for speculation.
He points to Bank of Spain figures from 2024 showing that only 8% of properties for rent are owned by companies.
Galindo says he concludes from the data available that there is not a notable accumulation of property to rent among a small number of owners in Spain.
"When it comes to explaining the rise in rentals, that is not the big cause," he says. "What explains it is the shortage of supply compared to demand over recent years."
The Bank of Spain appears to agree, and has estimated that the country has a housing shortfall of around 750,000 homes.
The institution's deputy governor, Soledad Núñez, warned in September that by 2028 that could rise to one million.
There are 3.8 million empty properties in Spain, according to the National Statistics Institute (INE), but a large number of those are in depopulated rural areas and therefore have little relevance to the current crisis, which is most acute in urban hubs.
Other explanations for this high number include properties awaiting renovation, or legal disputes between family members who have inherited them.
Demographic changes play a major part in the imbalance between supply and demand.
Between 2021 and 2025, there were about 1.2 million new households in Spain, driven in great part by the arrival of migrants who have played a major role in the country's recent economic growth.
However, house building has not kept pace, with fewer than half-a-million new homes during that period.
That was partly because Spain's construction industry had shrunk in the wake of the Eurozone crisis, while the cost of materials rose substantially after Covid, and a lack of political consensus put legal obstacles in the way of building.
"It was not a priority for us to build new houses," Galindo says. "But, once the demographic boom came, we realised how costly it was for us."
He adds that short-term tourist accommodation, like Airbnb, which has been identified by both the Spanish government and many activists as a culprit, is likely to have had a more localised effect, pushing up prices in specific urban areas rather than having an overall impact.
Meanwhile, the crisis has been aggravated by lagging salaries.
A study by El País found that, in real terms, the average Spaniard had 5% less spending power than a decade ago, due to taxes, social security and inflation. The average monthly salary in the Madrid region is €1,550 (£1,314; $1,738).
"No worker should have to spend 75% or 80% of their salary on rent, because what are they supposed to eat?" says Francisco Pardo, an 81-year-old retired taxi driver, who sympathises with the protesters, during a visit to the tent city in Madrid.
"Many workers don't even earn €2,000 [per month]."
The case of Maricarmen has suddenly made the housing crisis an urgent topic of discussion, not just in Madrid's Puerta del Sol but across the country.
The question now is whether a consensus can be reached on how to solve it.

articles.title: Europe's Energy Sector Must Close the Gap Between Cyber Regulation and Real-World Resilience - energynews.pro
articles.summary: Europe's Energy Sector Must Close the Gap Between Cyber Regulation and Real-World Resilience  energynews.pro
articles.full_text:
Europe's energy sector needs to close the gap between fast-evolving cyber threats and its ability to respond in practice, experts gathering today in Brussels for the 9th Cybersecurity Forum said. They argue that geopolitical attacks, artificial intelligence (AI) and the rapid growth of connected energy technologies create risks that regulation alone cannot address. Recent attacks on Poland's energy sector, Ukraine's experience and a live demonstration form the basis of the discussion.
A forum organised by four European players
The Forum is jointly organised by E.DSO (the European distribution system operators' association), EE-ISAC (the European energy Information Sharing and Analysis Centre), ENCS (a cybersecurity research organisation) and ENISA (the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity). It comes just weeks after the publication of ENISA's Threat Landscape 2026, which analysed 8,257 cyber incidents affecting EU Member States and EU-based organisations during 2025.
The report indicates that geopolitical developments continue to shape malicious activity. Attackers are also increasingly incorporating AI into their operations, and OT-related intrusion claims have increased. OT, or operational technology, refers to the systems used to control and monitor physical equipment and industrial processes. Power plant security questions also arise outside Europe: Libya is studying the use of regasified LNG for its power plants.
Lessons from Poland and Ukraine
The Forum is hearing first-hand accounts of the coordinated cyberattacks on Poland's energy sector in December 2025. They targeted numerous wind and solar farms, as well as a combined heat and power plant supplying heat to nearly half a million customers. Electricity generation was not disrupted, but communications between the affected facilities and distribution system operators were lost. The attackers had gained a level of access that could have enabled disruption.
NPC Ukrenergo, Ukraine's national electricity transmission system operator, is explaining how it is strengthening cyber resilience while operating a grid under sustained attack. The company uses AI to help its cybersecurity teams react faster, identify gaps, support staff and assist with reporting, while keeping critical decisions with people. Its experience also highlights the difficulty of maintaining specialist expertise, as skilled teams cannot easily be rebuilt through recruitment.
Connected devices, another point of vulnerability
The expansion of connected energy technologies creates a different challenge. ENCS researchers are demonstrating how an attacker who has already compromised an everyday smart-home device, such as a router or camera, could potentially use it to communicate with a residential solar inverter or home battery on the same network. Some of these devices use control protocols that do not authenticate who or what is issuing a command. An attacker may therefore not need to hack the inverter or battery itself to potentially influence whether it produces, consumes or stores electricity.
Compromising one household is unlikely to affect the grid, according to the presentation. Manipulating thousands of devices simultaneously, however, could create sudden changes in electricity generation or demand and potentially contribute to wider grid disturbances. Harm van den Brink, Security Researcher at ENCS, said: "More high-power IoT (internet of things) devices are being deployed every day, and vulnerabilities in some of these devices have already been exploited and could be exploited again to disrupt the electricity grid. In the short term, we need independent security testing, prioritised according to the amount of power potentially affected, combined with vulnerability management by manufacturers."

The Forum is examining how independent security testing, vulnerability management, information sharing and closer cooperation across the energy and cybersecurity sectors can help close that gap. The aim is also to keep limited specialist resources focused on the risks with the greatest potential impact.

articles.title: E.ON Next deal to buy Ovo Energy leaves UK with just ‘big three’ energy suppliers - The Guardian
articles.summary: E.ON Next deal to buy Ovo Energy leaves UK with just ‘big three’ energy suppliers  The GuardianE.ON completes acquisition of OVO  E.ON UKOvo energy customer? You'll be moved to E.on as a takeover deal has been agreed – here's what it means for you  Money Saving ExpertThe big six could become the big three after E.ON and OVO merge  Energy Live NewsThree Energy Firms to Supply Three Quarters of British Homes After E.ON-OVO Deal  Cornwall Insight
articles.full_text:
Almost three-quarters of households in Great Britain are now served by just three energy suppliers, after E.ON Next completed a deal to buy Ovo Energy despite fresh concerns about competition in the energy market.
The takeover concluded on Thursday after Britain’s competition watchdog cleared it, despite concerns that the shrinking number of household energy suppliers could mean bill payers will have less choice and suppliers will have less incentive to lower bills.
While there will be no immediate change for the 4 million households supplied by Ovo, the sale means that E.ON Next, which already supplies 5.6 million households, will hold 25% of the household energy market – or 13.45m gas and electricity accounts – and become Great Britain’s second-largest energy supplier.
The supplier’s hold on the market is narrowly behind Octopus Energy, which holds a 26% share or 14.3m accounts, and ahead of legacy energy incumbent British Gas, which was once the top supplier but today serves about 23% of the market or 12.5m accounts.
It also deals a blow to the decade-long efforts to dismantle the dominance of what were the “Big Six” energy suppliers to increase competition and lower energy prices.
Tom Goswell, the energy supply lead at Cornwall Insight, a leading consultancy, said: “The big six have become the big three, and there have been questions raised over how this will impact household choice and the health of the market.”
Those concerns were rebuffed by Chris Norbury, chief executive of E.ON UK, who described the market as “fiercely competitive” and said the company’s “flexibility and scale” would allow it to “deliver for customers now and to transform for the energy system to come”.
The legacy big six suppliers – British Gas, EDF Energy, E.ON UK, SSE, Scottish Power and npower – dominated about 85% of the energy market in 2016 when a landmark investigation by the CMA warned that customers were overpaying by roughly £1.4bn to £1.7bn every year due to weak market competition.
As a result of the E.ON deal, about 90% of Great Britain’s household energy supply market will be held by only five suppliers when including EDF Energy and Scottish Power alongside the big three.
Although there was a surge in new energy start-ups after 2016 – led by Octopus, Ovo and Bulb Energy – the market began to shrink after SSE sold its household supply business to Ovo in 2019, and dozens of suppliers went bust during the 2021/22 energy crisis.
Octopus became the biggest supplier in the market after taking on 1.5 million customers from Bulb, which became the biggest casualty when it went into administration in 2022.
“Larger suppliers do bring with them a degree of stability, and after about 30 firms dropped out of the market, leaving customers wondering who would be sending their next bill, stability is not something to dismiss lightly,” Goswell said.
“The concern with fewer suppliers is that the pressure to compete eases off, taking with it some of the incentive to keep prices low and offer something different. The big suppliers have the resources to give people real choice, and the test over the next few years will be whether households who shop around find a genuine range of deals waiting for them rather than three versions of the same thing,” he added.

articles.title: Will EU press the ‘kill switch’ on China? Trade war looms over talks - The Economic Times
articles.summary: Will EU press the ‘kill switch’ on China? Trade war looms over talks  The Economic Times
