articles.full_text:
HSBC is putting a raft of roles in its UK wealth division on the chopping block following a push to slash costs with artificial intelligence.
Europe’s biggest lender is consulting on changes to its wealth management operations that would lead to a shake-up for hundreds of relationship managers and financial advisers across the UK.
The move, first reported by the FT, could see the bank halve the amount of management and specialist roles it has and cut as much as 70 per cent of its financial advisers as part of the cuts.
HSBC does not disclose the total number of staff in its wealth operations. Its UK business has £134bn of wealth balances, which are roughly split equally across its private banking and premier banking businesses. Across the UK, it is estimated to employ up to 35,000 people.
Georges Elhedery, the bank’s chief, had previously urged the bank’s staff to avoid “fighting” its AI ambitions.
Staff must not be “disenfranchised, not anxious, overwhelmed, and resisting the change,” he told those attending an investor day event in May.
“We all know generative AI will destroy certain jobs and will create new jobs,” Elhedery said.
“But my initial mission is: I need 200,000 colleagues with us on this journey – however many will be left at the end of the journey isn’t the problem.”
Banks rush to AI for efficiency gains
HSBC is ranked first in the UK and 11th globally on the Evident AI index, which is used as a global benchmark to track banks’ AI capabilities.
Earlier this year, the bank’s peer Standard Chartered revealed plans to slash almost 8,000 back-office roles, stoking more fears of the consequences of AI on the financial services industry.
The lender’s boss, Bill Winters – one of the longest-serving FTSE 100 chiefs – pushed back against claims of “cost-cutting” and instead said it was “replacing, in some cases, lower-value human capital with the financial capital and investment capital we’re putting in”.
Winters later apologised for the comments in a lengthy LinkedIn post.
HSBC revealed a tie-up with Google Cloud earlier this year, where it aims to use AI to scout priority projects that could bank the firm $100m in “efficiency gains”.
The bank said in June the initial roll-out would focus on “hyper-personalised” wealth management, stronger financial crime risk management and AI tools to “enhance” client services.
City AM revealed in April that Lloyds had entered a deal with Google to build AI agents. Britain’s biggest mortgage lender sealed an agreement to use the tech giant’s suite of computing services to create a new internal platform for agents that will allow teams across its group to build their own tools and publish them to a central marketplace where other divisions can find and deploy them.
A spokesperson for HSBC said: “HSBC UK is a long-established, leading UK wealth manager and premium banking provider.
“We’re continuing to evolve to deliver more digitally-enabled products and journeys, to support our best-in-class wealth service and meet the changing needs of our customers.”

articles.title: Suspect linked to Monaco bomb attack on millionaire speaks to BBC from Ukrainian prison - BBC
articles.summary: Suspect linked to Monaco bomb attack on millionaire speaks to BBC from Ukrainian prison  BBC
articles.full_text:
A former Ukrainian security services officer linked to a bomb attack in Monaco in June that targeted a multi-millionaire says he believed it was ordered by senior members of HUR, Ukraine's military intelligence agency.
In an exclusive interview with the BBC from prison in Kyiv, facilitated by his lawyer, Vitalii Zhykovych has given his own account of the attempted assassination for the first time.
Ukrainian-born businessman Vadym Yermolayev and his 13-year-old son were badly hurt in the blast and his partner suffered catastrophic injuries. Yermolayev later described their survival as "nothing short of a miracle".
Zhykovych describes himself as a "freelancer" for Ukraine's SBU security service and says Anastasia Berezovska, the woman caught on camera planting the bomb in Monaco, was his "agent".
A week after the bombing, Berezovska's body was discovered in the woods west of Kyiv with gunshot wounds to the head.
But Zhykovych insists he did not send her to kill, and nor did he kill her.
He was arrested and accused of her murder together with an active-duty intelligence officer from HUR called Vladyslav Reut.
Reut initially confessed to investigators, and led them to the shallow grave. But days later in court, he changed his testimony to blame Zhykovych.
For a long time, Zhykovych himself stayed silent.
Now, responding to questions from the BBC, he alleges that Reut - who he refers to as "The Boss" - had "proposed the operation" in Monaco against Vadym Yermolayev.
He understood it was an official mission.
"As Reut informed me, this operation […] had been authorised and approved by Reut's superiors, who served in the Main Intelligence Directorate of the Ministry of Defence [HUR]," he says.
Distancing himself from the explosion itself, he alleges that Reut asked to use Berezovska for the bombing and when Zhykovych refused – he says she was not fully trained – Reut agreed to send her for reconnaissance instead.
Reut then communicated directly with Bereszovska without including him, according to Zhykovych, who alleges that Reut also provided her with the explosives.
The BBC asked HUR to comment on the latest claims. The agency has previously said that it is "committed to a full investigation" and providing "comprehensive support" to law enforcement bodies.
The SBU has described Zhykovych in a statement only as a "former law enforcement officer".
Yermolayev was attacked in Monaco as he and his family were returning from an evening meal on the seafront. A surveillance video shows Berezovska walking slightly in front of the group, then leaving the device in a bag on their doorstep.
It detonates just as they get close, apparently shocking even Berezovska with its force.
Yermolayev later said he believed that serving HUR officers, "individuals close to the agency's current and former leadership", were linked to the attack.
He called for "the truth, protection, and justice".
Berezovska was quickly identified as the suspected bomber and on 2 July her image, taken from CCTV footage, was circulated by Interpol.
She had already fled, first driving through Italy and Germany, then taking a bus from Frankfurt to Ukraine.
Before she could be caught and questioned though, she was driven to the woods by Reut and Zhykovych and killed. Each blames the other for her shooting.
The shocking case has prompted intense speculation, including over who may have wanted Yermolayev dead and why, and whether this could have been a state-ordered assassination attempt, a rogue operation or some kind of criminal score-settling.
The businessman himself, who renounced his Ukrainian passport some years ago and now has Cypriot citizenship, has dismissed multiple theories.
They include the idea the attack might be linked to a struggle between organised crime groups involved in highly lucrative scam call-centres in Ukraine.
Earlier this year, a court in Estonia convicted Yermolayev's son, Artur, of defrauding its citizens out of millions of euros through such "offisy", as the scam networks are known in Ukraine.
Vadym Yermolayev told the Ukrainska Pravda newspaper that he "never had anything to do with anything" in the case.
Now Zhykovych has put forward his own theory to us.
He alleges that Reut told him the bombing was in retaliation for "funding the annexation of Crimea", which he understood to mean Yermolayev was paying taxes to Russia from businesses in Russian-occupied Crimea.
"In my view, this constitutes grounds for the operation," he communicated from prison.
Yermolayev has repeatedly denied any remaining business interests linked to Russia.
But might this story be even murkier?
At his most recent custody hearing in Kyiv, surrounded by heavily armed guards, Zhykovych spoke publicly for the first time since his arrest. The BBC were the only media present.
At one point Zhykovych said Reut had in fact told him the attack in Monaco was not "authorised".
"Someone had ordered this target from the civilian side," Zhykovych said, without explaining.
The judge then interrupted, reminding him that he was addressing an open court.
Zhykovych also revealed that Reut originally talked of two targets.
When we asked, he said he could not disclose the second name. Other sources strongly suggest it was a pro-Russian blogger tried and convicted in absentia last year by Ukraine of treason.
As the investigation continues – into both the bombing in Monaco and the murder in Ukraine - Berezovska's family have many questions of their own.
The 39-year-old had been in Germany since early 2022, when she left Ukraine as a refugee with her young son.
Zhykovych now claims she was living a double-life, working with him as an agent "against Muscovy" – meaning Russia.
He said they had met online and told us the pair were working to "repel the armed aggression of the Russian Federation".
Berezovska's husband has told the BBC that the allegation was "nonsense". He believes she was dragged, unwittingly, into the whole affair.
Zhykovych says Berezovska called him the day after the Monaco attack, and when he asked why she had done it, she said Reut had promised her a huge fee. "$50,000 doesn't just lie on the streets," she supposedly explained.
Residents in her village have told us that Berezovska was saving to buy a flat. But when she travelled to Ukraine to collect the money, she was lured into the woods and shot.

articles.title: Intel Terafab deal survives TSMC takeover rumours ... - eeNews Europe
articles.summary: Intel Terafab deal survives TSMC takeover rumours ...  eeNews Europe
articles.full_text:
The Intel Terafab deal remains in place despite several days of speculation that TSMC could displace Intel from Elon Musk’s semiconductor manufacturing project. Intel chief executive Lip-Bu Tan confirmed the arrangement on Wednesday, while Musk separately rejected the idea that TSMC would take control of the planned fab. He said the facility would be built and operated by his companies, with TSMC potentially subleasing only part of the site.
Terafab is intended to secure advanced chip supply for Musk-linked businesses including Tesla, SpaceX and xAI. The latest statements leave Intel’s 14A technology at the centre of the manufacturing plan, but they also leave open the possibility of a separate TSMC operation on the same campus.
Intel Terafab deal keeps 14A in place
Intel became the first named semiconductor technology partner for the project earlier this year. As eeNews Europe reported in April, Musk said Terafab would use Intel’s next-generation 14A process and that SpaceX would take responsibility for high-volume manufacturing.
Intel has not publicly detailed the commercial structure of the arrangement, including whether Terafab will license the process technology, receive manufacturing assistance from Intel, or both. Intel’s current process information describes 14A as using second-generation RibbonFET gate-all-around transistors and PowerDirect backside power delivery, with the node aimed at next-generation AI and high-performance computing designs.
The customer relationship also matters strategically to Intel. The company has previously said that leading-edge process development needs substantial external wafer volume to make the economics work. In 2026 it committed to completing 14A development while continuing to seek major outside customers. A large Terafab deployment would give Intel a prominent external use case, although no committed wafer volumes or financial terms have been disclosed.
TSMC sublease would be technically awkward
Musk confirmed discussions with TSMC earlier this week, which triggered speculation that the Taiwanese foundry might own or operate the facility. His latest comments narrow that possibility considerably: Terafab would remain under his companies’ control, while TSMC could potentially lease part of the site for its own production.
That would be an unusual arrangement. Advanced fabs are not interchangeable cleanroom shells. Each foundry uses proprietary process flows, tool configurations, materials, metrology, automation, yield-management systems and contamination controls. A TSMC production line sharing a campus with Intel-derived 14A manufacturing would therefore need strong physical, operational and intellectual-property separation. In practice, it could look more like a separate fab inside the wider Terafab site than a conventional sublease.
TSMC also has its own competing technology roadmap. The foundry says A14 is scheduled for volume production in 2028, while it continues a major expansion of its US manufacturing base in Arizona. No agreement for TSMC participation in Terafab has been announced.
Texas project moves beyond the concept stage
Partner roles may still be fluid, but the physical project is advancing. The state’s August announcement said SpaceX would build the first phase of Terafab in Grimes County, Texas, with more than US$16.8 billion of capital investment and 3,000 jobs. Local filings have described a substantially larger possible multi-phase build-out, but those later phases should not be treated as committed spending.
For now, the Intel Terafab deal has survived the TSMC takeover speculation. Intel remains involved, TSMC has not been given control of the project, and Musk is insisting that operating responsibility will stay with his companies. Whether TSMC accepts any sublease role, and how such an operation could coexist technically and contractually with Intel 14A manufacturing, remains unresolved.

Well, it was fun for the Chinese while it lasted. But as Andy Burnham has reportedly been warned by German chancellor Friedrich Merz that rejoining the EU will not be possible unless the UK raises tariffs on Chinese electric cars to 45 per cent, the days of a Jaecoo sitting at the top of the sales charts may be long gone. Or will they?
The complications of cosying up to China and the EU are huge. So far, we’ve been hoping that being relatively tariff-free has boosted trade relationships with China – a market that’s crucial for British car brands and likely to be one of the most lucrative for the new Jaguar Type 01, for example – and encouraged Chinese investment in the UK.
But that pathway means the EU, who Burnham seems keen to grow stronger ties with and even potentially rejoin, might not include British-made cars in its ‘Made in Europe’ plans which could mean additional incentives offered to people who buy eligible vehicles.
Politics is tough, isn’t it?
Let’s look at what happened when Trumps tariffs first hit: did prices for British-made cars suddenly skyrocket in the US? Well, you’ll be surprised how much room there is for car makers to take a bit of the burden, which is exactly what happened and that’s what may well happen with the mega-rich Chinese car makers.
And not all tariffs are the same. Across the EU, car makers that are owned by the state, or those that don’t co-operate with the EU’s anti-subsidy investigation, are hit the hardest. MG owner SAIC, for example, sits in the highest band as it’s Chinese government owned and gets the full 45 per cent tariff.
What does that do for prices? An MG4 Urban – the entry into MG’s electric car range, lists at €27,190 in Germany, which equates to around £23,000. The same car in the UK costs from £23,495. Tariff? What tariff?
As for other Chinese car brands, privately-owned BYD gets hit with a total of 27 per cent in tariffs, with Geely at 28.8 per cent. Prices don’t seem to be much higher in Europe for those cars, either.
We all know how quickly the Chinese move when it comes to developing and launching new cars, and they’re being just as quick when it comes to European production, which will get around tariffs for the biggest-selling models that are planned to be built in Europe.
Building a new factory isn’t the work of a moment, although BYD’s Hungarian factory is coming on stream in what looks like record time. Others are using more cunning plans, with Chery talking to Nissan about using its Sunderland plant for production, as well as looking at production in Spain.
Spain seems popular as Leapmotor is talking to its co-owner Stellantis about building cars at the existing Madrid and Zaragoza factories – and sharing tech that will mean new Vauxhalls could well use Leapmotor platforms, too. SAIC is also rumoured to be looking at Spanish production.
Geely has the advantage of owning Volvo, which has factories in Sweden, obviously, but also Belgium. It also owns Lotus, which has done plenty of engineering work on Geely models, while Chinese state-owned Changan has had a research and development facility in the UK for years.
So, what will the impact be of tariffs on Chinese cars coming into the UK? Looking at what’s happening in Europe, my guess would be not much. We may see prices for Chinese-made models rising a touch, which isn’t exactly what you want to see in a competitive market. It’ll be interesting to see if European brands follow suit and use it as an opportunity to raise prices, too.
What may well happen is we see the acceleration of local production from Chinese car makers – although that’s unlikely to be the UK. Some years ago when Tesla opened its Berlin factory, I asked Elon Musk why he didn’t consider the UK for a factory. His response was simple: Brexit made it too difficult.
Burnham needs to turn on the charm with the EU and the Chinese to have any chance of a Chinese car maker doing a Nissan or Toyota and build cars here. Honda turned tail and disappeared pretty quickly.
One thing we do want to avoid is scaring Chinese car makers off. It may be unlikely, but the last thing we’d want is for all those Jaecoo owners to have nowhere to take their cars for servicing or repairs. And although these new brands aren’t building cars in the UK, many are employing a great many people in their British operations and through their retailers.
It’s a difficult balancing act, but I don’t see the Chinese car makers going anywhere anytime soon – they’re in it for the long haul, more brands are planning to come to the UK and, judging by the sales numbers, Brits seem to be very happy to buy Chinese.

articles.title: So Goes Europe - American Thinker
articles.summary: So Goes Europe  American Thinker
articles.full_text:
Britain is America's mother country. Regardless of what one may think of the once-Great Britain today, much of America's essence sprang from that island's political philosophy, cultural inheritance, legal tradition, and national character. Our language, common law, conception of liberty, parliamentary instincts, and stubborn individualism all trace back directly to Britain. Britain may have declined, but the DNA of its greatness lives on in us. Its decline is therefore not merely a foreign story. It is a cautionary tale written in a language we understand because we inherited it. We ignore those linkages at our peril.
Margaret Thatcher represented perhaps the last great demonstration of Britain's willingness to behave like a world power. The Falklands War was not merely a military victory; it was a psychological one. It proved that Britain still possessed the will to act decisively, defend its interests, and project power beyond its shores. For a moment, Thatcher restored something of the Churchillian confidence Britain had lost before that moment too faded away.
She could not reverse the forces already embedded in the country's institutions. The political class increasingly embraced managerialism, the intellectual class fashionable self-doubt, and the bureaucracy technocratic caution. Britain turned inward, consumed by domestic demands and increasingly skeptical of the burdens of global leadership. Its decline was not simply imposed from outside. A nation that loses confidence in its own purpose eventually loses the political will to sustain it.
That is where the parallel to America becomes unavoidable.
Britain became increasingly burdened by internal social obligations that expanded faster than its economic capacity and political will. America has accumulated similar burdens for decades. However noble their original purposes, domestic obligations expand, demand resources, and rarely contract. A great power cannot be defined solely by what it redistributes. It must also be defined by what it builds, protects, and leads. When internal obligations consume the resources and political attention required for those purposes, national power begins to erode into irrelevance.
But Europe's problem is not simply that its governments became more cautious or its welfare states ever more expensive. Europe also changed itself. Over the past several decades, large-scale immigration has transformed the demographic and cultural composition of countries built around relatively strong national identities and shared expectations.
Immigration becomes more difficult to absorb when it is large in scale, communities become concentrated, assimilation weakens, and governments become increasingly reluctant to insist on a common civic culture. Nations have always absorbed newcomers. The difficulty arises when newcomers can establish durable communities organized around languages, customs, religions, or social expectations distinct from those of the larger society -- and when the state hesitates to insist that legal entry, assimilation, and adherence to common laws and institutions are the price of belonging.
France illustrates the scale of the transformation. In 2024, 7.6 million immigrants lived in France, representing 11.2 percent of the population. In 1968, nearly three-quarters of foreigners living in France were European nationals; by 2024, nearly half were African nationals and only about one-third were European.
Those numbers do not prove social failure on their own. They do, however, describe a profound demographic transformation. When that transformation occurs alongside concentrated communities, weakened assimilation, and the state's reluctance to insist on a common civic framework, demographic change becomes a source of social and political friction rather than simply population growth.
And this is where immigration intersects with the larger problem of European decline. A confident state can absorb substantial change because it knows what it expects of those who enter it. A state that has lost confidence in its own culture, doubts its right to demand assimilation, and fears the political consequences of enforcing its laws has a much harder task. The question is no longer simply how many people a country can admit. It is whether the country still possesses the confidence and authority to insist that everyone living within its borders belongs to the same civic order -- and what it must do when some refuse.
France may be showing us the next stage.
What makes the French crisis particularly dangerous is the convergence of three different pressures against the state: the red -- economic grievance; the white -- cultural conflict; and the black -- violence and disorder. The red attacks its economic legitimacy. The white attacks its cultural legitimacy. The black attacks its monopoly on force. They are not a coalition or even a unified movement. Together, they constitute a stress test.
When those pressures erupt simultaneously, a parliamentary system built around compromise and negotiation becomes incapable of meeting the moment, hesitating when it must act and debating when it must decide. It fears backlash when it must assert authority.
The danger is not necessarily that the French state will be overthrown. It is that it will surrender functionally -- by narrowing its ambitions, avoiding confrontation, tolerating disorder, and accepting that certain neighborhoods, groups, or behaviors are beyond its reach.
That is how decline accelerates, not through dramatic collapse, but through the quiet acceptance of limits that did not previously exist.
And, in the wings, our own Red, White, and Black forces are taking notes. America cannot simply watch Europe decline from across the Atlantic. The lesson of WWII is that geography no longer protects a nation from the collapse of the civilization to which it belongs. Had America simply assumed that events across the Atlantic could never threaten us, the history of the twentieth century might have been very different. Oceans provide distance, not immunity.
Europe is not simply another collection of foreign countries. It is the civilization from which we emerged. If Europe loses the capacity to govern itself, defend itself, assimilate newcomers, and maintain the institutions that made the West prosperous and free, America may eventually discover that it is next.
This is not a prophecy of America's future, not yet, but it is a warning.
Great nations do not remain great by accident. They remain great because their people choose renewal over resignation, responsibility over retreat, and courage over comfort. America still has the economic, military, cultural, and political capacity to help Europe regain its footing and, in the process, ensure our own stability.
We should do so not out of nostalgia or charity, but self-interest.
Europe helped create the civilization that made America possible. As the elder child, America now has a responsibility to help preserve it -- not because Europe is entitled to American protection, but because a weakened Europe ultimately weakens the West.
If Europe recovers, America's foundations are strengthened. If Europe continues to decline, America will eventually discover that oceans are no substitute for civilization.
So goes Europe.
God Bless America.

Two commercial vessels were hit within 24 hours — one off Qatar, the first attack in that area in six months, and one off Fujairah in the Gulf of Oman — as IRGC-affiliated outlets suggested Tehran had extended operations beyond the crucial strait.
Iran's armed forces struck two commercial tankers outside the Strait of Hormuz within 24 hours this week, in what appeared to be a deliberate expansion of attacks beyond the strait, as Iranian officials issued a fresh wave of warnings against the United States.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said several projectiles hit the oil and chemical tanker Acers, flagged in Antigua and Barbuda, 51 nautical miles north of Madinat ash Shamal in Qatar on Wednesday. Casualties were reported.
Maritime intelligence firm Vanguard identified the vessel and said it was heading toward the Strait of Hormuz.
It was the first attack in that area in more than six months.
In a separate incident on Thursday, Vanguard reported a fire on a tanker some 40 kilometres off Fujairah in the Gulf of Oman, which it identified as likely the Marshall Islands-flagged Dhalgout.
The UKMTO had not recorded the incident, and the cause of the fire was not immediately clear. NASA's FIRMS fire-detection system confirmed the blaze, and US military aircraft — including two KC-46 tankers, a KC-135, a P-8A maritime patrol aircraft and several helicopters — were over the area at the time.
Iran and media affiliated with the IRGC did not officially claim responsibility for either attack. IRGC-affiliated outlets implicitly suggested that Tehran had "extended the scope of its operations against commercial vessels that violate Iranian laws and regulations in the Strait of Hormuz to waters beyond the strait."
Both incidents fall outside the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly one-fifth of global oil and gas shipments normally pass. The strait has been effectively closed since the war began in late February, after Iran and the US imposed concurrent naval blockades.
"The distance between you and us is determined by our missiles," Acting Defence Minister Majid Ebn ol-Reza posted on X on Thursday.
"Yesterday the Gulf of Oman, today the Indian Ocean and tomorrow the Bay of Pigs. If you make a mistake, you will see a new set of dividing lines.," ol-Reza added in an apparent reference to a failed, US-backed military landing on the southwestern coast of Cuba from April 1961 aimed at overthrowing the communist government of Fidel Castro.
Yahya Rahim Safavi, a senior military adviser to Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, had earlier warned that if the US or Israel attacked Iran again, Tehran could extend the war "as far as the Indian Ocean or other places," adding that Iranian forces had prepared contingency plans for worst-case scenarios.
Ebn ol-Reza was appointed acting minister after Aziz Nasirzadeh, Iran's then defence minister, was killed on 28 February — the first day of the war — alongside several other military commanders. Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has nominated Mehrdad Akhlaqi as a permanent replacement, and parliament is due to hold a confidence vote on 18 October.
Iran's army spokesman said separately that its forces were ready to carry out pre-emptive operations, if necessary, to prevent what he described as "any aggression or attack by the enemy."
At a midterm election campaign rally in Nebraska, US President Donald Trump defended the decision to go to war with Iran. "This is a small price to pay for keeping the world and our country safe. They can destroy a city. Let them destroy it. Let them destroy Los Angeles, let them destroy San Diego," he said.
At a separate rally in Texas on Wednesday night, Trump walked back those remarks after criticism. "We protect our own cities. We will not allow such a thing to happen," he said.

articles.summary: EU presses Russia for more details on suspected plague case  Euronews.comWhy a global outbreak of pneumonic plague is unlikely  BBCWHO says it does not have ‘full picture’ from Russia following suspected plague death  The GuardianOpinion | Here’s What Worries Me About the Russian Plague Scare  The New York TimesRussia denies second case of infectious disease - as WHO seeks to verify reports of new 'plague' contact  Sky News
articles.full_text:
Pressure mounts on Moscow to explain the suspected plague case in Siberia, which has put health authorities on edge. Brussels is calling on Moscow to come clean with precise details "as soon as possible".
The European Commission has stepped up pressure on Russia to provide full details of a suspected plague case in Siberia, echoing calls for transparency from the United States and the World Health Organisation (WHO).
Moscow has pushed back,insisting there is no risk of an epidemic.
"Let me say, for the third time this week in the press room: Russia should make information about the plague available as soon as possible," Eva Hrncirova, the Commission's health spokesperson, said on Thursday.
"We don't have enough information to assess the epidemiological situation, to assess the risks for other countries and to take appropriate measures, if necessary."
The comments came a day after the Commission convened the EU's Health Security Committee, bringing together representatives of the 27 member states, along with the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) and the WHO.
The committee coordinates the EU's response to serious cross-border health threats, allowing national authorities to share information, assess risks and discuss possible measures.
However, Wednesday's meeting ended without any specific decisions because of the lack of reliable information from Russia.
The Commission said it was ready to reconvene the committee at short notice if new information emerged or the situation deteriorated.
"We need information from Russia," Hrncirova said. "It's linked to the Russian membership in the WHO Europe: sharing timely, precise, exact information so that the experts can assess the situation because the situation can have cross-border implications."
The EU delegation in Moscow reached out to the WHO's office in Russia to convey its concerns, the spokesperson said, citing the lack of direct diplomatic contact between Brussels and Moscow since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
"Basically the whole world is waiting for the information from Russia," she added.
The case revolves around a female lab worker at the Irkutsk Research Anti-Plague Institute, in south-eastern Siberia, who died on 2 October in uncertain circumstances.
Her death was initially attributed to a "pneumonia of unknown aetiology", sparking global alarm and intense scrutiny.
Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's public health watchdog, says the lab worker was "vaccinated and had immunity to the dangerous infections she was working with", and that nearly 5,000 laboratory tests had detected no dangerous pathogens.
More than 90% of those who had contact with her have completed medical monitoring after being placed under strict observation, it said.
WHO has requested details to clarify the lab worker's death, the pathogen that triggered the quarantine measures, and a reported second case, which Moscow called "false".
The US has also urged Russia to provide accurate and timely information. President Donald Trump said he had scheduled a call with his Russian counterpart, Vladimir Putin, to discuss the suspected outbreak.
"We have officially requested additional information from the Russian government. We are also in official communication with other countries around the world to share information," a US State Department spokesperson said.
Pneumonic plague occurs when the bacteria responsible for plague infect the lungs. It is the most serious form of the disease and can spread from person to person. Without treatment, its case-fatality ratio ranges from 30% to 100%.

articles.full_text:
The just-released minutes of the ECB’s September meeting confirm that the decision to raise interest rates by 25bp was driven by a deteriorating inflation outlook
By the time the ECB met in September, a 25bp rate hike had already come to be seen as the most likely outcome. The just-released minutes of that meeting show that the ECB’s Governing Council was united in its view that a worsening inflation outlook and economic resilience called for a hike. The minutes, however, give a less hawkish picture than ECB president Christine Lagarde’s comments at the press conference.
Here are the most relevant phrases from the minutes:
Worsened inflation forecast the reason for the rate hike. The updated staff projections indicated that inflation was set to remain well above target for an extended period. Increasing the deposit facility rate from 2.25% to 2.50% was a robust decision across a wide range of scenarios. While measures of underlying inflation had shown little change so far, the full inflationary impact of the energy shock had yet to play out.
Some ECB members pointed to less inflation drama. It was pointed out that the energy shock could be less persistent than assumed, as it was essentially a politically driven shock that could disappear as quickly as it had appeared.
And not all members were fully supportive of the resilience narrative. It was still too early to draw a firm conclusion about the degree of resilience of the economy on the basis of the latest growth figures.
The risk of the knock-on effects of higher energy prices on the rest of the economy remains. Rising energy prices could also transmit to food prices. In addition, higher fertiliser prices precipitated by the energy shock, together with the impact of El Niño and recent heatwaves, could put upward pressure on food commodity prices.
But there have been few indirect effects so far. Indirect effects had remained contained and second-round effects had not been seen. It was also suggested that a cooling labour market and moderating wage growth could limit the risk of second-round effects.
On France. Not a single word. Only that a further rise in long-term interest rates could adversely affect growth.
The concept of a neutral interest rate does exist. While it was noted that the response should remain proportionate, it was also pointed out that a deposit facility rate of 2.50% remained in the range of neutral interest rates estimated by staff.
No forward guidance. Against this backdrop, communication should remain neutral, neither suggesting that the current decision was another step in a predetermined tightening cycle nor that it was the last rate hike. At the same time, continued vigilance was vital.
All in all, the minutes show an ECB that saw no risk in hiking rates at the September meeting, but looking ahead was more balanced than the comments at the press conference suggested.
French fiscal situation will push ECB to be more dovish
The next ECB meeting is in three weeks. So far, there is little reason to believe that the bigger macro picture will change significantly until then. Maybe with one exception: the rise in bond yields and the fiscal situation in France. The surge in German bond yields since the September meeting has already had the same impact on growth and inflation as an additional 25bp rate hike. For France, it's closer to a 50bp hike. With bond markets doing the ECB's job, some officials might be less keen to continue hiking than they were at the September meeting.
The ECB’s October meeting doesn’t look like a meeting to discuss further rate hikes. This will be for the December meeting. However, the October meeting could facilitate a more general discussion on how to react to the current French situation and speculations by some market participants on a new eurozone sovereign debt crisis. Here, we see three potential policy responses: the first was already prepared by Lagarde during her comments at the European Parliament: easing the hawkish tone and possibly agreeing on fewer rate hikes than markets had priced in. The second is the end of Quantitative Tightening and a restart of reinvesting matured bonds. This could bring some relief to bond markets. The ECB could even decide to purchase eurozone debt but not French debt, in case France is not able to pass a budget compliant with the European fiscal rules. And the third, and more distant, option would be to start the Transmission Protection Instrument. It would be more outright asset purchases, aiming at narrowing spreads.
In any case, it looks as if the hawks from the September meeting might find themselves as more collateral damage from the French fiscal mess.

articles.full_text:
The Home Office has confirmed a new October passport rule at 13 airports across the UK. As of October 6, new contactless technology will be introduced at eGates across UK airports to help speed up security checks and deliver smoother journeys for passengers. The change means that passengers arriving in the UK will soon pass through airport eGates securely without having to show their passport, with the new contactless system upgrade due to complete at every eGate by early 2027.
Rather than having to manually scan passports at eGates, or show them to Border Force officers, passengers will instead simply approach the eGates and have their photo taken. The system will then check this live image against verified immigration, travel and passport information, and the eGate will then open automatically once these checks are complete.
The Home Office said the contactless system uses state-of-the-art facial comparison technology to verify a passenger’s identity before the UK’s robust border security checks are carried out in full. Legitimate travellers can then simply walk through, without needing to place their passport on the eGate reader.
If further checks are required, passengers will then have to place their passport on the reader or they may be directed to a Border Force officer, as is currently the process. Border Force officers will continue to monitor all eGates to offer assistance and passengers are advised to keep their passports with them at all times.
According to the Home Office, testing shows the new contactless system is up to 25% faster than using a passport on an eGate. It comes after the Home Office changed the age limit for passengers who can use UK eGates back in July to include children aged eight and nine years old who are at least 120cm (3ft 11in) tall.
Phil Douglas, director general of Border Force, said: “This is a win for travellers coming to our brilliant country. By using state-of-the-art technology, we are making journeys smoother and faster, all while fully maintaining the UK’s robust border security.
“Our digital transformation also builds on our work this summer to extend eGates to children aged eight and above, making life a little easier for families.”
The contactless system will be introduced in phases, with the rollout starting at East Midlands Airport, initially for British Citizens, before expanding to more airports and other nationalities already eligible for eGates over the coming months.
Steve Griffiths, managing director of East Midlands Airport, said: “We’re delighted to be the first UK airport to have contactless eGates introduced by Border Force.
“As an airport committed to providing an effortless travel experience, we welcome any technological innovation that can help to safely make our customers’ journeys smoother, swifter and simpler.
“This complements changes that we carried out to our immigration hall recently to help improve the flow of arriving passengers through the area.”

Bristol
Cardiff
East Midlands
Edinburgh
Gatwick

articles.title: Deloitte hit with £11m fine after missing £30m taxpayer fraud at UK transport giant - City AM
articles.summary: Deloitte hit with £11m fine after missing £30m taxpayer fraud at UK transport giant  City AMSee more headlines and perspectives on Google News
articles.full_text:
Big Four giant Deloitte has been fined £11m for failing to raise concerns about fraud in its statutory audits of the transport business, the Go-Ahead Group (GAG), which operates multiple train services across the UK.
The Financial Reporting Council (FRC) said on Thursday the fine, which was discounted to £6.05m for early admission and co-operation, related to the Big Four giant’s audit of the transport firm between the 2016 and 2020 financial years.
GAG, a major transport group, provides rail and bus services across the country, and from 2016 to 2020, the group was listed on the London Stock Exchange. The group is London’s largest bus operator, running roughly a quarter of the capital’s buses across 17 depots on behalf of Transport for London (TfL), including the Elizabeth Line.
The breaches relate to three of GAG’s subsidiaries that operated passenger rail services: London and South Eastern Railway Ltd (LSER), London and Birmingham Railway Ltd (LM), and Go-Ahead Bayern GmbH (GABY). The findings on Deloitte’s failure to apply “professional scepticism” regarding three subsidiaries. The regulator found that, in each case, Deloitte accepted management’s explanations without sufficient challenge.
The FRC said Deloitte, across all three subsidiaries, failed to recognise that it had wrongfully retained over £30m in taxpayer funds by keeping overpayments to the Department for Transport (DfT), and it failed to address the transport group’s concerns.
The Big Four firm also received a severe reprimand alongside the fine and an order to prepare a report for Deloitte’s FRC firm supervisor explaining why these failures happened. The regulator said Deloitte must pay the full costs of the FRC’s investigation.
“These breaches show a highly concerning pattern of failure by Deloitte to apply sufficient scrutiny to decisions and actions by GAG which were clearly questionable. The fact that some of those decisions and actions put very large amounts of UK taxpayers’ money at risk is particularly troubling, and this is reflected in the high level of financial sanction imposed,” said Penrose Foss, executive counsel and executive director of investigations and enforcement.
Commenting on the fine, a spokesperson from Deloitte UK said: “We regret that aspects of our audit work did not meet the standards expected and have learned from this matter. We are committed to continuous improvement and the delivery of high quality audits.”
Regulator drops Joules probe
Separately, the regulator also announced on Thursday that it closed its probe into Deloitte over its audit of former listed lifestyle brand Joules Group.
The FRC launched the investigation in May 2023 after Joules collapsed into administration in late 2022, reviewing the audit for the year ended 30 May 2021.
The British fashion retailer, founded by Tom Joule, collapsed into administration on 16 November 2022. A month later, retail giant Next partnered with founder Tom Joule to acquire the business out of administration in a £34m to £41m deal.
After a “review of the evidence and all relevant factors” from Deloitte’s audit of the business, the FRC closed its investigation into the Big Four giant without taking any enforcement action.

Yemeni government forces have said they “neutralised” 1,860 Houthi fighters since launching a large-scale counteroffensive to retake territory under the control of the Houthis, an armed group also known as Ansar Allah or Supporters of God.
The spokesperson for the internationally recognised government’s military said in a social media post early on Thursday it had carried out 2,103 “precise targeting operations” against Houthi military positions across several fronts as part of the ongoing “Dawn of Yemen” campaign.
The Yemeni government, backed by Saudi Arabia, also says its forces have captured strategic mountain positions in western Taiz overlooking the coast.
Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, announced on Sunday the Dawn of Yemen operation to retake all Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the Iran-backed group has controlled since 2014.
Battles in Yemen have focused in recent days on areas around the Bab al-Mandeb strait, a shipping route that has become more crucial for energy exports since the US-Israel war on Iran restricted trade through the Strait of Hormuz.
Forces aligned with the Yemeni government launched an operation on Tuesday to recapture strategic territory near the strait and around the city of Mocha, which the Houthis had taken last month.
Coalition targeting
The Saudi-led coalition fighting in Yemen said on Wednesday it destroyed 82 Houthi military targets in the Yemeni governorates of Saada, Hodeidah, al-Jawf and Marib.
The spokesperson for the coalition said in a statement that the targets included missile sites, including “11 mountain-based ballistic missile storages in Saada, command and control centres, communication systems, missile and weapons storages”.
The latest operation followed Houthi attacks on Tuesday and Wednesday targeting King Khalid international airport in Riyadh and Abha international airport, according to the spokesperson.
The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation (GACA) said the attacks on the two airports killed three people.
One person was killed and eight were wounded in an attack on King Khalid airport, while two people were killed and 28 were wounded in the attack on facilities at Abha airport, the GACA said in a statement.
The attacks have drawn condemnation from across the region. Kuwait denounced the attacks as a “flagrant violation” of Saudi sovereignty and international law. Egypt said the attacks threaten the security of the entire region.
The Mecca-based nongovernmental organisation Muslim World League also condemned the strikes, describing them as “treacherous terrorist attacks”.
As the fighting rages on, Yemen’s permanent representative to the United Nations, Abdullah al-Saadi, met the UN secretary-general’s special envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, on Wednesday to discuss the situation in the country.
During their talks, al-Saadi accused the Houthis of rejecting peace initiatives and de-escalation efforts proposed by the Yemeni government.
He stressed that the government’s goal is to extend its control across the entirety of the country and end the Houthis’ ability to wage war. He said the government is seeking a permanent end to the war and is not interested in a temporary truce, arguing that such a scenario would only lead to fighting later.

Why some cities become leading AI hubs
An AI cluster is more than a concentration of technology companies. It is a connected ecosystem in which AI businesses, startups, skilled talent, research institutions, investors, infrastructure providers and supporting organisations interact and reinforce one another.
These ecosystems may extend across an entire metropolitan area or form within a specific innovation district, technology hub or university-led research cluster.
Colliers’ analysis of AI clusters in Europe identifies four critical foundations for success: government-led initiatives, startup ecosystems, universities and research institutions, and Big Tech laboratories. Data centre capacity provides an increasingly important supporting layer, particularly for organisations developing and training advanced AI models.
The strength of an AI cluster does not depend on any single ingredient. It comes from the connections between them.
Universities provide AI talent, research and commercial opportunity
A strong university sector provides the AI talent, research capability and commercial connections needed to support a successful ecosystem.
Universities educate skilled graduates, attract international researchers and generate new intellectual property. Their value also lies in connecting academic research with commercial organisations, investors and entrepreneurs.
This relationship helps ideas move from research into practical AI applications, new businesses and employment. Universities can also attract Big Tech laboratories seeking access to researchers, specialist expertise and opportunities for collaboration.
Europe’s leading AI cities demonstrate the importance of this connection. Their universities and research institutions do not operate in isolation. They form part of wider technology ecosystems that link education, innovation and commercial growth.
Startup ecosystems turn innovation into businesses
Research capability alone does not create a successful AI cluster. Cities also need the entrepreneurial capacity to turn ideas into viable products and companies.
Strong startup ecosystems provide access to founders, investment, accelerators, advisers and experienced technology professionals. This infrastructure helps early-stage AI companies establish themselves, recruit talent and scale.
Venture capital plays a particularly important role. Funding allows AI startups to invest in specialist talent, infrastructure and product development before they have established predictable revenues. A visible pipeline of growing companies can then attract further investors and skilled workers, reinforcing the ecosystem.
Different European AI clusters reflect different models. Berlin is distinguished by its startup culture and entrepreneurial environment, while Stockholm combines strong startup activity with research capability.
Big Tech laboratories strengthen local AI ecosystems
Big Tech laboratories are research and development centres operated by major technology companies. Examples identified in the report include Google DeepMind, Meta AI and Microsoft Research.
Their presence can strengthen an AI innovation hub by creating skilled employment, supporting collaboration with universities and contributing knowledge to the wider business community.
Large multinational organisations can also give emerging AI companies access to capital, data, technology infrastructure, specialist talent and international markets. This creates opportunities for collaboration across different technologies, industries and areas of expertise.
However, the presence of major technology companies is most valuable when it complements local research and entrepreneurship rather than operating separately from them.
Government initiatives can accelerate AI cluster growth
Public policy has an important enabling role in successful AI ecosystems.
Government support can include investment in research, skills, digital infrastructure and technology commercialisation. Policy institutions and clear regulatory frameworks can also provide businesses and investors with greater confidence.
The European Commission aims to mobilise €200 billion through its InvestAI initiative, including €20 billion for AI gigafactories. Nineteen AI factories are also planned as innovation hubs intended to support collaboration and development across the broader European AI ecosystem.
Public funding does not create a successful AI cluster on its own. It is most effective when it strengthens existing relationships between research institutions, talent, businesses and investors.
Data centre capacity supports advanced AI development
AI increasingly depends on access to substantial computing power, cloud connectivity and resilient digital infrastructure.
Data centre capacity is particularly relevant to Big Tech laboratories and companies training advanced AI models. It complements the four foundations of an AI cluster by providing the technical infrastructure needed to develop, test and deploy AI systems.
Nevertheless, infrastructure alone is not enough. A city with significant data centre capacity but limited specialist talent, research activity or startup formation is unlikely to develop the same depth of AI ecosystem as a city where these elements operate together.
Successful AI clusters create reinforcing cycles of growth
AI clusters are developing across Europe in major office markets and smaller academic and specialist centres. Within this wider network, London, Paris and Berlin are emerging as the leading hubs, while a second tier is developing in Munich, Zürich, Amsterdam, Dublin, Stockholm, Warsaw, Barcelona and Helsinki. Beyond these established hubs, Madrid, Milan and Copenhagen are emerging as specialised AI clusters, building on local academic expertise and established technology and industrial strengths.
Their strengths differ, but the underlying principle is consistent: successful AI clusters connect people, ideas, capital, infrastructure and commercial opportunity.
For businesses and occupiers, these ecosystems provide access to talent and networks. For investors and developers, they indicate where new economic activity and office demand may become concentrated.
The cities best positioned to benefit from Europe’s expanding AI economy will not necessarily be those with the largest individual investments. They will be those that create the strongest connections between research, entrepreneurship, technology and talent.

articles.title: Silicon Valley of Europe: Why Its Tech Hubs Don't Add Up - Startuprad Io
articles.summary: Silicon Valley of Europe: Why Its Tech Hubs Don't Add Up  Startuprad Io
articles.full_text:
Is there a Silicon Valley of Europe? Not one, but several strong hubs: Zurich and Upper Bavaria around Munich are in the EU's top 5 of 241 innovation regions. The weak point is between them. On joint research papers, the European Commission scores Europe's hub network at 0.76 against America's 0.81. On joint patents, Europe falls to 0.40 against 0.68.
What Is This About?
This is Part 7 of The European Scale-Up Question. In the last 18 months the EU has published three sets of numbers that belong together: a ranking of Europe's most innovative regions, its first startup and scale-up index for every member country, and a study on how well Europe's innovation hubs connect. Read side by side, they raise one question for every founder in Germany, Austria and Switzerland: when the capability your company needs sits in another hub, what stands between you and using it?
The video goes live on Thursday, October 8th, 2026
Europe does not need to build startup ecosystems from scratch. It already has them. The question is what it costs a company in one strong region to use what the others have. That is the thread running through our startup scaling playbooks for Germany, Austria and Switzerland, and it is the thread of this series.
In Parts 1 to 5 of The European Scale-Up Question we looked at bottlenecks one at a time: fragmentation as a hidden growth tax, capital that breaks between rounds, public money that funds supply but rarely becomes a customer, and operators who do not recycle into new companies. In Part 6, Capital Gravity, we followed companies moving their parent company, their CEO and their capital relationships to America.
This episode tests a hypothesis, not a law of nature: several of those bottlenecks are also problems of access between hubs. Not all of them. Several.
One correction on the record. In Part 5 we cited the figure that 56% of startups founded by unicorn alumni are started in the same city as the unicorn. That figure comes from Dealroom's 2022 data and covers Europe and Israel together. The figure is real. The year and the region matter.
Executive Summary
Europe has excellent innovation regions, and two of the EU's top five, Zurich and Upper Bavaria, are in the DACH region. National conditions are more average: Germany ranks 14th of 27 on the EU's new startup and scale-up index. The strongest evidence on links between hubs comes from a 2025 Commission study: European hubs collaborate almost as closely as American hubs on research, and much less on patents. That does not explain the whole scale-up gap, but it points at a cost founders pay when the capital, people or customers they need sit across a border.
Key Takeaways
Europe's problem is not a lack of strong hubs. It is the cost of reaching what the other hubs have.
The gap is smallest in research (0.76 vs 0.81) and largest in commercial invention (0.40 vs 0.68).
Physical distance in Europe is small. Institutional distance, meaning borders, currencies, tax, employment law and registries, is large.
Germany, Austria and Switzerland together are a place to learn and win pilots, not a substitute for scale.
Run The Network Test on the next capability your company needs, and count the cases where it worked too.
Europe Already Has Strong Regions
The EU's Regional Innovation Scoreboard 2025 covers 241 regions. 38 are rated Innovation Leaders and 69 Strong Innovators. Between 2018 and 2025, performance rose in 233 of the 239 regions that could be compared. The top five: Stockholm, the Copenhagen region, London, Zurich and Upper Bavaria.
This ranks regional innovation systems, meaning research, skills and companies investing in innovation. It is not a ranking of startup cities. But two of the top five sit in our home markets.
The national picture is different. On the EU's new European Startup and Scaleup Scoreboard, Germany ranks 14th of 27, at roughly the EU average. That is not a contradiction. Big federal countries have strong and weak regions; a region can be excellent while national conditions around it are average. Europe overall improved by 13.5 points on that index between 2020 and 2025. That is an index score, not 13.5% more startups, and the Commission still names late-stage money as a constraint.
The Framework: Ecosystem Density and Ecosystem Connectivity
Two ideas carry this analysis. Ecosystem Density is how much startup capability sits inside one hub: founders, angels, universities, seed funds, early customers. Ecosystem Connectivity is how easily a company can use what sits outside its home hub: an investor in Stockholm, an industrial customer in Munich, an engineer in Paris.
A company starting out mostly needs density. A company scaling needs both, because almost no single city has every investor, executive and customer it will need between 50 and 500 employees. The balance depends on sector and stage.
The Evidence: Research Connects, Invention Does Not
The best evidence is the Commission study Divided we fall behind (June 2025). Its researchers mapped collaboration between 168 European and 144 American urban areas from 2000 to 2023. "Europe" here includes the UK, Switzerland and Norway.
The index compares the links hubs actually have with a benchmark of the links you would expect from each hub's size. 1 is a perfect fit. It is not a percentage of links achieved.
When European scientists in different hubs publish together, Europe scores 0.76 against America's 0.81. When inventors patent together, Europe falls to 0.40 against 0.68.
Europe's hubs are physically closer to each other than America's, so distance alone does not explain the gap. What separates Munich from Zurich is not the train ride. It is a border, a currency, a tax system, an employment law and a separate patent and company registry. Boston to San Francisco crosses a continent, but inside one currency, one securities regulator, one patent office and one capital market.
The study also finds that European collaboration clusters inside national borders, and that the gap with America is widest in complex technologies such as AI, biotech and quantum computing.
What the data does not show: it measures invention networks, not whole businesses. An investor can back a company abroad without a shared patent. Part of America's higher score may come from US companies running teams in several hubs under one parent. The study names possible causes, including national rules, language and legal and tax frameworks, without ranking them.
The Strongest Objection
Perhaps Europe's real problem is that too few hubs have enough growth capital, large customers and experienced leaders, and connecting them will not create resources that are missing everywhere. That objection is partly right: if a resource does not exist in Europe, no bridge helps.
But when a resource does exist, the extra cost of reaching it across a border is real, and the founder pays it. The Commission's October 2025 study on venture and growth capital funds describes Europe's markets as still fragmented and lists legal, tax and market barriers to cross-border investment. More money behind the same borders makes every hub richer. It does not make them easier to reach.
Five Areas, Five Founder Decisions
Capital. Before your next round, look beyond your home network for investors who understand your sector and can back your next stage. Ask every fund whether its mandate lets it invest in your country and how much it reserves for follow-on rounds. A fund that loves you but cannot follow you is not your lead.
People. When you hire leaders for the 50-to-500 stage, start from the capability gap, not the postcode. Check early what it takes to employ someone, and give them equity, in the countries you are likely to hire from.
Customers. The IMF has estimated that barriers inside Europe work like a tariff of around 44% on goods and 110% on services. The IMF calls that an upper bound, and other economists dispute it, but the friction is not imaginary. Choose your second market where you have the strongest evidence of demand and a credible way to sell, not where the train is shortest. Austria or Switzerland can be a cheap place to learn and win a pilot. But do not mistake Germany, Austria and Switzerland for scale: together they are still smaller than the home market of an American competitor.
Organisations that make this easier to reach, such as funds investing across DACH, corporates buying from startups in other countries, and regions courting founders, can work with Startuprad.io to reach exactly these founders and investors.
Know-how. Munich, Zurich, Eindhoven, Grenoble, Stockholm and Cambridge can each specialise, but only if companies can reach them. Find the best partner for the capability you lack, at home or abroad, and settle IP ownership in writing before joint work starts.
Company structure. Once a year, ask the Capital Gravity questions: where is our parent company, where does our CEO work, where are our senior commercial hires, where do we expect to list? If answers are moving west, write down why.
Superclusters Are Proposals, Not Proof
Dealroom has argued for treating the hubs within four hours by train of London as one supercluster, and has sketched a second around Munich. Drawing a circle on a map does not mean a company can use what is inside it on the same terms. The real test case for our listeners is Munich, Vienna and Zurich: two of Europe's top five innovation regions, three countries, and Switzerland outside the EU.
The Network Test
Instead of asking every region to build its own Silicon Valley, run this test on your own company. For the next capability you need, find the best option at home and the best option elsewhere. Can you actually use the outside option? What extra time, cost or eligibility rule comes with it? What would change if that friction disappeared?
Only count things your company actually needed. Moving the whole company should not be the only way to get access. And count the cases where it worked. T
