articles.summary: Oil tops $105 as Trump weighs return to Iran combat operations  Euronews.comTrump Says U.S. Will Not Strike Iran Again Before Midterms as Military Draws Up New Plans  The New York TimesTrump says he doesn't want Iran deal as U.S. reportedly prepares for 'massive bombing'  CNBCU.S. military prepares new Iran war options ahead of midterm elections  NBC NewsTrump readies new Iran strikes as Strait of Hormuz attacks ramp up  The Telegraph
articles.full_text:
Brent crude rose above $105 a barrel on Thursday after reports that US President Donald Trump is considering a return to "major combat operations" against Iran, while European stock markets opened lower as rising oil prices fuelled inflation fears.
The global benchmark for oil prices jumped by about 5% as traders braced for a possible new US offensive against Iran, piling pressure on equities already rattled by climbing borrowing costs.
Brent was over $105.2 a barrel in early afternoon trading in Europe, while US benchmark West Texas Intermediate (WTI) gained 5.1% to around $92.75.
American media reports on Wednesday indicated the Pentagon had instructed US Central Command to complete preparations for a possible resumption of "major combat operations" against Iran, citing US officials.
No date has been set for any strikes, which could hit Iranian energy, infrastructure and nuclear sites, according to the report.
An Israeli official told Axios that the chances of an attack before next month's US midterm elections were "not high but we don't rule it out".
Reportedly, even supporters of the strikes did not expect them to bring Iran to the negotiating table or restore safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz, but hoped they would help US President Donald Trump project strength before the midterm elections.
The US and Iran have yet to reach a deal to end their war, which began in February.
Supply worries were already mounting. Tehran has stepped up attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, the Houthis denied claims they had lost key territory, and senior oil officials have warned that global reserves are running worryingly low.
Output has also been hit in the US, where producers have shut down more than 500,000 barrels a day of Gulf of Mexico production ahead of Hurricane Isaias.
Crude prices had fallen earlier in the week on signs that Middle East exports were heading back towards pre-war levels and after G7 nations agreed to tap their stockpiles.
On Wednesday, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said its members supported speeding up oil stock releases already pledged in March, prioritising diesel where possible.
Stocks slide as inflation fears return
European stock markets opened lower on Thursday as the jump in oil prices revived inflation concerns. At the open, Germany's DAX fell 0.76% and London's FTSE 100 dropped 0.75%. France's CAC 40 was down 0.64%, while the Euro Stoxx 50 lost 1.06%.
Higher oil prices also added to upward pressure on government bond yields, which have reached multi-year highs. In the morning, France's 10-year yield stood at 4.89% and Germany's at 3.48%, while the 10-year US Treasury yield hovered near a multi-decade high at 5.32%.
Rising yields tend to weigh on stocks, as higher borrowing costs can squeeze company profits and make bonds more attractive to investors.
Minutes of the US Federal Reserve's September meeting, released on Wednesday, showed most officials considered another rate hike likely to be appropriate before the end of the year.
The Fed hiked rates in September for the first time since July 2023, by a quarter of a percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4%, as US inflation remains above its 2% target.
Markets across Asia fell, including Tokyo, Hong Kong, Sydney, Shanghai, Singapore, Seoul, Wellington, Taipei and Manila.
Samsung shares dropped despite the company estimating a 782.5% rise in third-quarter operating profit to 107.4 trillion won (about €71.8 billion), driven by higher memory chip prices.
On Wednesday, Wall Street's S&P 500 slipped 0.2% a day after hitting an all-time high. The Dow Jones Industrial Average lost 0.7%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite fell 0.2% from its record.
Tech shares pulled back as investors prepared for earnings season, with high valuations and vast spending on artificial intelligence putting profits under scrutiny.
The euro stayed near the 17-month low it hit on Monday, weighed down by concerns over France's high debt levels. On Thursday morning, the euro traded at $1.12, the pound at $1.32 and the dollar at ¥158.13. Gold edged up to $4,143.90 an ounce.
Investors were also awaiting the European Central Bank's account of its latest policy meeting for clues on whether it will hike rates again.

articles.title: UK’s military needs to focus spending on domestic defence, not overseas missions – report - The Guardian
articles.summary: UK’s military needs to focus spending on domestic defence, not overseas missions – report  The Guardian
articles.full_text:
The UK’s military is too focused on global commitments at the expense of domestic defence, meaning the government’s planned increase in defence spending is likely to result in even greater waste, a thinktank report has warned.
According to an analysis by researchers at the Transition Security Project, Britain has the most overseas-oriented military among European nations, with almost a quarter of the defence budget spent on commitments across five continents.
Calling this a symptom of a “destructive, outdated foreign policy” centred on overseas missions that have often made the world less safe, the report says ministers should prioritise changing their approach rather than immediately increasing spending, with resources shifted from overseas commitments to domestic defence.
The government is committed to spending 3.5% of GDP on defence by 2035 and a defence investment plan (Dip) was unveiled in July at the tail end of Keir Starmer’s premiership.
Starmer’s defence secretary John Healey resigned over a refusal to commit to reaching 3% by 2030, but now that Healey is chancellor that target has been shelved for now.
It would involve a doubling of the defence budget in nominal terms from £70bn in 2026 to £151bn in 2035, according to the Transition Security Project, a research centre that was spun out of Common Wealth, a thinktank with close links to Andy Burnham.
Using figures from 2024-25, the study estimated that about 23% of the military budget for that year was spent on overseas commitments, costing just over £14bn, with the real figure likely to be higher. About £2.8bn was spent on deployments used to project force outside Europe, including bases in places such as Cyprus, Kenya and Oman and elsewhere as “strategic hubs” for projecting UK military power.
The report says this makes the UK the most overseas-committed military among European Nato members, even if France has more personnel posted abroad. The Dip seems unlikely to reverse this, talking about continuing commitments on other continents.
The report questions whether more of the new money should be used for domestic defence, and whether the focus on overseas missions has made the UK safer. Since 2001, the study says, the UK has spent more than £51bn in modern terms on military interventions in Iraq, Afghanistan, Libya and elsewhere.
“Britain’s decision to maintain a global network of military bases and force projection capabilities, combined with high levels of waste in the military procurement system, raise serious questions about how it is allocating public investment,” it says, urging the government to “review its military posture, prioritising defence over the global projection of military force”.
Kevin Cashman, a researcher at the Transition Security Project who co-authored the report, said: “Britain should not pour more money into a bloated military sector geared towards alignment with the United States while Washington starts wars around the world that drive up our bills.”
Khem Rogaly, a co-director of the organisation and also a co-author, said: “The billions of pounds Britain wastes on global military deployments every year symbolise its destructive, outdated foreign policy. Britain should end its support for these attempts at global policing. Instead, it should focus its military resources on defence and its public investment on health, housing and the climate emergency.”
There is an awareness among defence officials of the importance of avoiding waste, including the risk that an arbitrary focus on reaching a certain level of spending could exacerbate this.
The intention is to focus instead on what is necessary – primarily on preparing the UK for a possible war in Europe.

articles.title: Ford F 150 holds US sales crown, stays off European roads - RUSSPAIN.com
articles.summary: Ford F 150 holds US sales crown, stays off European roads  RUSSPAIN.com
articles.full_text:
Ford’s F 150 has led US pickup sales for 44 years, packing up to 430 horsepower and towing over 6,100 kilos. Despite its dominance, the truck remains a rare sight in Europe.
On any given day, the Ford F 150 rolls out of American dealerships in numbers that dwarf the competition. The truck’s grip on the US market has lasted four decades, fueled by brute strength and a design that fits the country’s appetite for big, capable vehicles.
Ford’s own specs show the F 150 lineup starts at 325 horsepower and tops out at 430, but those numbers only tell part of the story. The 3.5-liter EcoBoost engine, rated at 382 horsepower, is the one that unlocks the highest towing figure—13,500 pounds, or about 6,123 kilos. The hybrid PowerBoost version pushes output to 430 horsepower, yet its maximum tow rating drops to 11,600 pounds. Ford’s documentation spells out the caveats: cab style, drivetrain, axle ratio, equipment, and payload all shift the numbers. Buyers chasing the top spec won’t get every headline figure in a single truck.
Europe, meanwhile, never gets a taste. Ford keeps the F 150 out of its showrooms, steering European buyers toward the Raptor and other models. The reasons are blunt: the truck’s size and thirst for space clash with narrow roads and dense cities. Local regulations and buyer habits push the company to focus elsewhere.
Look closer at the split. In Spain and across much of Europe, drivers have traded in sedans for SUVs, but pickups never caught on. The US doubled down on trucks and 4x4s, filling highways with vehicles that would barely squeeze through a Paris side street. The F 150’s scale and swagger simply don’t translate.
Automotive tastes split further as electric SUVs flood Europe. The BYD Great Tang, for example, has racked up record sales and is now eyeing a European launch, according to recent industry reports. The F 150, by contrast, stays put in the US, its absence in Europe underlining the gulf in what buyers want and what roads can handle.
Ford’s playbook is clear. The company builds for the market in front of it. What sells in Texas or Michigan rarely fits Madrid or Paris. European models get tuned for local rules and infrastructure, while the F 150 remains a US icon—oversized, unapologetic, and built for a different kind of driver.
Industry data shows the F 150’s reign is rooted in the specific demands of American buyers. In Europe, the truck’s absence signals a market that prizes different strengths. The F 150’s story ends at the border, its legend sealed on home turf.

articles.title: Adidas sues Australian label White Fox over four stripes design - BBC
articles.summary: Adidas sues Australian label White Fox over four stripes design  BBCAdidas sues Australian label White Fox over ‘deceptively similar’ four-stripe clothing  The GuardianAdidas takes White Fox to court over four-stripe clothing designs  News24Adidas Sues Independent Australian Brand for Trademark Infringement  Daily Front RowFashion feud: Adidas aims to tear stripes off White Fox  Newcastle Herald
articles.full_text:
Adidas is suing Australian label White Fox for selling and advertising clothes with a four-striped design, arguing it is "deceptively similar" to the German brand's distinct logo.
The sportswear giant said it had repeatedly asked White Fox to stop selling and promoting the clothes since March, but the Sydney-based company refused.
The fast-fashion online retailer is popular with teenagers and young adults in Australia, the UK and the US, and has relied on billboards, bus advertising and influencers - often university-aged - to grow its profile.
In the Federal Court on Friday, lawyers for White Fox denied any breach of trademark.
While White Fox has not yet lodged a formal defence, its lawyers told Justice Ian Jackman that the firm intends to argue that other prominent Australian brands such as Cotton On, Sportscraft and Glassons sell clothes with "similar decorative stripes".
Lawyers for Adidas told the court that White Fox, in advertising and selling its clothes with four stripes, had the "intention to trade off our reputation".
A three to four-day trial is expected to take place early next year, the court heard.
In its written statement of claim, Adidas says its three-striped design has a "substantial and valuable reputation" in Australia, where it has been trademarked since 1957.
The company says since at least March, White Fox has been selling and advertising clothes with four parallel stripes of equal width, which it claims is an infringement of Adidas's trademark.
White Fox's designs are "substantially identical with or otherwise deceptively similar" to Adidas, the company claims.
It also argues that White Fox's advertisements for its four-striped clothes and White Fox-branded socks feature people wearing "genuine" Adidas items.
This might lead Australians to think Adidas is associated with White Fox and has approved of the design, the documents claim.
The company says White Fox is "drawing an association in the minds of consumers" of the two brands, or at least "sailing close to the wind".
Adidas, which reported €24.8 billion (£21bn; $28bn) in revenue in 2025, is also seeking damages, saying White Fox must pay them the profit from the products plus interest and costs.
Evidence provided by Adidas included side-by-side comparisons of its products with White Fox clothes which include sweatpants and lounge shorts, as well as images of billboards on buses and at bus stops.
In one example, Adidas claimed that an online listing from June 2025 showed a pair of White Fox-branded socks being modelled by someone wearing pink Adidas shoes.
A few days after the court proceedings were lodged last month, the Adidas logo on the shoes were digitally altered to remove one of the stripes, the documents alleged, and a week later, all three stripes were scrubbed from the image.
In 2013, Adidas successfully sued Pacific Brands in Australia for selling shoes with four stripes.
White Fox was launched in 2013 by Georgia and Daniel Contos and is privately-owned by the Greek-Australian couple and Daniel's mother Melina Maceri. It has a growing presence in the US and expanded into the UK market in 2024.
In the 12 months to June 2025, the company generated AU$542m (£286m; $377m) in revenue, a four-fold jump from its 2022 figure of $121m, according to the Australian Financial Review.

Birmingham Airport announces £2bn expansion
Birmingham Airport has announced a £2bn expansion plan which bosses say could more than double passenger numbers and create thousands of jobs.
The draft plan, a spokesperson said, sets out the use of existing runway capacity alongside "significantly enhanced" passenger facilities over the next 15 years.
Unveiling an eight-week public consultation, chief executive Nick Barton said the scheme aims to ensure the airport was "ready for the future" but needed a "fair and stable taxation environment".
Transport secretary Heidi Alexander said the government was "backing our aviation sector to continue growing, right across the country".
In 2025, the airport said it had seen a record year with more than 13 million passengers travelling through it. Bosses want to see this rise by more than double, up to 30 million a year.
Airport chiefs said the proposals set out a "clear commitment" to continue serving the region and create more than 50,000 jobs, including 3,800 at the airport site.
They added that they wanted to make sure the growth was "delivered responsibly and sustainably" for the people living closes to the site.
The first stage of development could start in 2027, with significant investments in areas such as baggage and terminal facilities, additional aircraft stands and improvements in surface access.
Hundreds of passengers were affected by issues with the airport's baggage system in August, with many left without their luggage.
People can give feedback on the plans online, by post or attend any of the 20 events, which start in Hampton on Arden on 16 October.
"The £2bn proposed investment is unprecedented at Birmingham Airport and will take our airport close to 30 million passengers," said Barton.
"This level of ambition sends a strong signal of support and confidence in our airport and wider region.
However, Barton added that the plan came at a time the airport was faced with increased running costs from wage bills, energy prices and taxation.
"Unless tax and regulatory environments are made more favourable and stable for major infrastructure investment, they [the plans] may not materialise," he said.
Alexander said the city's plan was a "massive boost" to the West Midlands, unlocking investment and "creating 50,000 well-paid local jobs to get people into employment".
Richard Parker, the Labour mayor of the West Midlands, also welcomed the "ambitious masterplan" which he said would improve international links and unlock vital backing for local businesses and supply chains.
"This consultation gives local people and business owners a chance to have their say and help shape the airport's expansion so that it brings lasting benefits for our communities," he said.
